title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
content_c:
Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
- Published
Riot police have been deployed at Poland's Constitutional Court amid an escalating stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.
The row pits the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk against his predecessors from the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS).
The police intervention came after Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had requested stripping the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.
Tusk has vowed to depoliticise the judiciary, and on Friday defended the move as PiS supporters gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw in protest.
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has now entered the constitutional court, according to his chief of staff.
Nawrocki cancelled a trip to Senegal mid-air in order to attend to the confrontation in Warsaw. He had been on his way to the Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar.
Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.
In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.
Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.
The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.
Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Justice Minister Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.
Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.
"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.
  - Published2 June 2025
  - Published5 June 2023

title: 'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
content_c:
'No nation left behind' says Burnham after meeting first ministers in Glasgow
- Published
The prime minister has said the UK's four nations must "move together" to devolve more power to regions and cities, following a meeting with the Scottish and Welsh first ministers in Glasgow.
Andy Burnham said he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind" after the sit-down, which also included representatives from Northern Ireland.
SNP leader John Swinney said he welcomed recognition that "Westminster is not working for Scotland" and pledged to work "constructively and collaboratively" with Burnham, while Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iowerth said the meeting was "positive".
Both first ministers have called for a wider conversation about independence but Burnham has ruled out referendums.
- Scotland 'not like Manchester', Swinney says in dig at PM Burnham 
  - Published17 October
- Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution' 
  - Published16 October
- First minister says Budget not serious about Wales ahead of meeting with PM 
  - Published13 hours ago
Speaking after the first National Economic Council for the nations in Glasgow, Burnham highlighted plans for devolution at the regional level, saying he wanted to ensure no nation was "left behind".
"It's really important we all move at the same pace together, and I won't allow anything to delay that," the prime minister said.
"Growth can't wait. People need to see improvements in employment and in living standards in all parts of the UK."
Northern Ireland was represented by officials at the meeting amid the political fallout from the Drumcree parade dispute.
Ministers and representatives at the summit discussed handing regions more powers to control employment support and funding for reindustrialisation.
"It's about creating those structures at a regional level and that is matter for Scotland and Wales to decide what that looks like in both countries," Burnham said.
He urged the Scottish and Welsh governments to "work jointly" with the UK government on "a model of deeper devolution".
In the context of reindustrialisation, Burnham added this could be more devolution of innovation funding.
Swinney, ap Iorwerth and Burnham also agreed during the meeting there are too many young people out of work in the nations.
The prime minister said the UK government would look at "arrangements for further devolution of employment support for young people in both Scotland and Wales".
Devolution has been at the heart of Burnham's policy agenda since he took his place in Downing Street this summer.
He claims "rewiring the state" and handing more control to regional mayors and authorities across England will boost economic growth.
The prime minister's devolution at the national level has so far been less clear but Burnham has said he will listen to the administrations' calls for further powers while advocating that they share more responsibilities with local authorities.
'Welcome start'
John Swinney said while he and Burnham disagree on independence, the meeting was "a welcome start" on further devolution.
"When the people of Scotland take issues into their own hands, the best outcomes will about," Scotland's first minister said.
"To that end, I will work constructively and collaboratively with the prime minister to devolve more powers from Westminster to Scotland - as long as those proposals drive economic growth that is felt in higher wages, better jobs, more opportunities for business to start and expand, and support with the cost of living."
A Downing Street spokesperson said the UK government would review issues raised by the first minister but this would not include a second independence referendum in Scotland.
Rhun ap Iowerth said: "I was pleased to meet with the prime minister in Glasgow today where I once again pressed the need for Wales and the Welsh government to have the necessary tools to better serve our communities.
"I also reiterated the point that further devolution within Wales is a matter for the Senedd and only the Senedd."
He added he welcomed the prime minister's "step forward" on the Welsh government's fiscal and borrowing powers and gave his "full support" in pushing for a stronger relationship with the EU.
The prime minister had "positive discussions" with the Welsh leader, Downing Street said.
A spokesperson added: "The first minister of Wales agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

title: Yorkshire Water boss resigns after firm downgraded
content_c:
Yorkshire Water boss resigns after firm downgraded
- Published
Yorkshire Water's chief executive has announced she is to step down, just 24 hours after the company was given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency.
Nicola Shaw, who has led the firm since 2022, will leave the role on 1 January to be replaced by Nicola Medalova, a chartered environmental health officer who previously worked for the National Grid.
In a statement on Friday, Shaw said it had been a "privilege" to lead the company but that it was the "right time" to leave her post.
Shaw has faced criticism in recent years, including for taking £1.9m in undisclosed payments between 2023 and 2026, while the company has come under scrutiny for its performance.
The payments were made by Yorkshire Water's parent company, Kelda Holdings, for what the firm said was "investor engagement" and "financial oversight".
On Thursday, the Environment Agency gave the firm one star out of four - its lowest possible rating - meaning Yorkshire Water was classed as a "poorly performing company".
The EA said Yorkshire Water was responsible for 260 pollution incidents in 2025, which was its highest total since 2011.
In 2024, Ofwat announced it was fining the company £47m for historic sewage leaks.
'Extremely proud'
In her statement, Shaw said: "It has been a privilege to lead Yorkshire Water and serve the people of Yorkshire.
"Although there remains a huge amount of work to do, I am extremely proud of what our colleagues have achieved, putting the business on a stronger footing for delivery across all aspects of its work."
Yorkshire Water said Medalova, who is a former non-executive director of the company's board, would join the firm on Monday as part of a transition period before assuming the chief executive officer role full time in the new year.
She said: "I am delighted to be joining Yorkshire Water and grateful to the board for the opportunity to lead the business through its next chapter.
"Yorkshire Water faces huge challenges but also great opportunities for continued improvement and I look forward to working with Nicola Shaw, the leadership team and colleagues across the business as I get up to speed."
In December last year Shaw said "not being transparent" about receiving £1.3m in shareholder-funded payments across two instalments had been a "mistake", but had insisted those amounts were "not for me to decide".
She received a further £660,000 earlier this year. Ofwat said the payments were not performance-related.
The previously undisclosed payments had come to light the previous August when the government banned Yorkshire Water and five other water companies from paying "unfair" bonuses to bosses.
Reaction from MPs and campaigners
Tom Gordon, Liberal Democrat MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, said Shaw should have stepped down "much earlier".
"Good riddance. Nicola Shaw oversaw abysmal management of our precious natural resources, trashing our rivers while receiving an eye-watering salary," he said.
"Her replacement needs to understand that residents are at their wits' end, paying ever-rising bills for polluted rivers and threats of hosepipe bans while someone at the top rakes in millions."
Meanwhile, Judith Cummins, Labour MP for Bradford South, said Yorkshire Water needed "more than a change of leadership" but a "complete change of direction".
"A new face at the top cannot wash away years of Yorkshire Water failing to put customers first," she said.
"Nicola Shaw's time as Yorkshire Water boss saw customers frustrated by poor service, skyrocketing bills, record pollution incidents, and a plummet from 'good' to the worst possible one-star environment rating.
"There must be a wholesale shift in culture that finally prioritises customers. Only then can the company begin to restore public trust."
Robbie Moore, Conservative MP for Keighley and Ilkley, said Shaw's resignation "could not have come quick enough".
He added: "I have therefore already requested an urgent meeting with the new CEO Designate Nicola Medalova to understand how she plans to improve Yorkshire Water's performance at speed.
"The status quo cannot continue."
Chris Stewart at York campaign group Ouse It Lose It said the new CEO's priority had to be looking at "failures in the system".
"There's been a continual decline in the operation of this business," he said.
"Clearly things are going wrong."
Stewart said he was not surprised by Shaw's resignation but it was a "shocking indictment of the way the company has been performing, while making loud noises about how much they're putting into improving".
Naomi Tilley, campaigns manager at protest group Surfers Against Sewage, said "systematic change" was needed to fix the company.
"Regardless of who the CEO is, there's sewage entering the sea and the water companies are failing. Yorkshire Water is not an outlier," said Tilley.
"The whole system and every water company is failing in different ways and we are seeing that the system is broken and we need fundamental change.
"While these companies are set up for a profit, we're never going to see pollution curbed and stopped."
Additional reporting by David Rhodes and Grace Wood

Yorkshire Water's chief executive has announced she is to step down, just 24 hours after the company was given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency.
Nicola Shaw, who has led the firm since 2022, will leave the role on 1 January to be replaced by Nicola Medalova, a chartered environmental health officer who previously worked for the National Grid.
In a statement on Friday, Shaw said it had been a "privilege" to lead the company but that it was the "right time" to leave her post.
Shaw has faced criticism in recent years, including for taking £1.9m in undisclosed payments between 2023 and 2026, while the company has come under scrutiny for its performance.
The payments were made by Yorkshire Water's parent company, Kelda Holdings, for what the firm said was "investor engagement" and "financial oversight".
On Thursday, the Environment Agency gave the firm one star out of four - its lowest possible rating - meaning Yorkshire Water was classed as a "poorly performing company".
The EA said Yorkshire Water was responsible for 260 pollution incidents in 2025, which was its highest total since 2011.
In 2024, Ofwat announced it was fining the company £47m for historic sewage leaks.
'Extremely proud'
In her statement, Shaw said: "It has been a privilege to lead Yorkshire Water and serve the people of Yorkshire.
"Although there remains a huge amount of work to do, I am extremely proud of what our colleagues have achieved, putting the business on a stronger footing for delivery across all aspects of its work."
Yorkshire Water said Medalova, who is a former non-executive director of the company's board, would join the firm on Monday as part of a transition period before assuming the chief executive officer role full time in the new year.
She said: "I am delighted to be joining Yorkshire Water and grateful to the board for the opportunity to lead the business through its next chapter.
"Yorkshire Water faces huge challenges but also great opportunities for continued improvement and I look forward to working with Nicola Shaw, the leadership team and colleagues across the business as I get up to speed."
In December last year Shaw said "not being transparent" about receiving £1.3m in shareholder-funded payments across two instalments had been a "mistake", but had insisted those amounts were "not for me to decide".
She received a further £660,000 earlier this year. Ofwat said the payments were not performance-related.
The previously undisclosed payments had come to light the previous August when the government banned Yorkshire Water and five other water companies from paying "unfair" bonuses to bosses.
Reaction from MPs and campaigners
Tom Gordon, Liberal Democrat MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, said Shaw should have stepped down "much earlier".
"Good riddance. Nicola Shaw oversaw abysmal management of our precious natural resources, trashing our rivers while receiving an eye-watering salary," he said.
"Her replacement needs to understand that residents are at their wits' end, paying ever-rising bills for polluted rivers and threats of hosepipe bans while someone at the top rakes in millions."
Meanwhile, Judith Cummins, Labour MP for Bradford South, said Yorkshire Water needed "more than a change of leadership" but a "complete change of direction".
"A new face at the top cannot wash away years of Yorkshire Water failing to put customers first," she said.
"Nicola Shaw's time as Yorkshire Water boss saw customers frustrated by poor service, skyrocketing bills, record pollution incidents, and a plummet from 'good' to the worst possible one-star environment rating.
"There must be a wholesale shift in culture that finally prioritises customers. Only then can the company begin to restore public trust."
Robbie Moore, Conservative MP for Keighley and Ilkley, said Shaw's resignation "could not have come quick enough".
He added: "I have therefore already requested an urgent meeting with the new CEO Designate Nicola Medalova to understand how she plans to improve Yorkshire Water's performance at speed.
"The status quo cannot continue."
Chris Stewart at York campaign group Ouse It Lose It said the new CEO's priority had to be looking at "failures in the system".
"There's been a continual decline in the operation of this business," he said.
"Clearly things are going wrong."
Stewart said he was not surprised by Shaw's resignation but it was a "shocking indictment of the way the company has been performing, while making loud noises about how much they're putting into improving".
Naomi Tilley, campaigns manager at protest group Surfers Against Sewage, said "systematic change" was needed to fix the company.
"Regardless of who the CEO is, there's sewage entering the sea and the water companies are failing. Yorkshire Water is not an outlier," said Tilley.
"The whole system and every water company is failing in different ways and we are seeing that the system is broken and we need fundamental change.
"While these companies are set up for a profit, we're never going to see pollution curbed and stopped."

title: How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programme
content_c:
North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.
Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.
North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.
Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.
A UN panel of experts, reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.
The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.
The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.
Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match.
“Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one,” Martin said.
North Korea was behind one of the last large cyber thefts on a traditional bank – an attack on Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, where North Korean hackers tried to illicitly move $951m from an account the bank had with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, taking advantage of time differences between the two.
A piece of luck prevented most of the money from being sent to an intermediate account in the Philippines. The corresponding bank was based on Jupiter Street, which shares its first word with the name of a sanctioned Iranian ship, so most of the transfers were held up. In the end, $81m was stolen.
The isolated state has long been accused of engaging in criminal activities to survive, including the forgery of high-quality $100 bills, known as “supernotes” in the 1990s, and the production and trafficking of crystal meth for export in the 2000s.
The UK has been rarely targeted. In 2019, North Korean hackers did try to take control of cash machines linked to 56 financial institutions to make them pay out sums well in excess of normal. British officials spotted what was afoot, alerted the banks and the hack was quietly suppressed with no media coverage.
The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.
Hacking is closely tied to the all-powerful state. In December 2014, it emerged, to the embarrassment of Sony Pictures, that film stars Jennifer Lawrence and Amy Adams were paid less than their male counterparts in American Hustle. It was one of thousands of embarrassing emails leaked from the Hollywood studio through a hack.
The attack, by North Korea’s Lazarus Group, was conducted because Sony had funded a film, The Interview: a Seth Rogen comedy that depicted the assassination of Kim Jong-un. Amid the chaos of the revelations, Sony tried to cancel the movie, then had to U-turn on its retreat, releasing it online and to a handful of cinemas, after being criticised for caving in to North Korean pressure.

title: Public sector an ‘afterthought’ to North Sea oil jobs, says Unison leader
content_c:
The leader of the UK’s biggest trade union has called for the same political focus to be given to NHS, education and care sector workers as there has been on those employed in North Sea oil and gas.
Andrea Egan, the general secretary of Unison, said too often public sector workers were treated as an “afterthought” by the government compared with the “massive political focus” on protecting jobs in the North Sea.
“There’s no question it is vital for oil and gas workers to be guaranteed secure, well-paid jobs in the industries of the future,” Egan said. “But public service workers, in contrast, often seem like an afterthought for ministers. What about the thousands of jobs cut in recent years across local government, the NHS and education? Care workers, nurses, teaching assistants.”
North Sea oil and gas has been in the headlines again in recent weeks after the government gave the go ahead to the Jackdaw gasfield following huge pressure from the fossil fuel industry and rightwing politicians – in the UK and abroad.
The decision caused anger among climate campaigners and scientists, as well as many Labour supporters, who argue that extracting more fossil fuels will further escalate the crisis and do nothing to reduce bills, significantly improve energy security or halt the long-term decline in jobs in the sector. A final government decision on the more controversial Rosebank oilfield is expected before the end of the year.
After Wednesday’s budget, which factored in the project’s approval in its forecast, the Guardian revealed some Labour MPs were lobbying Andy Burnham and John Healey not to overrule the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, if she decided to block Rosebank.
Egan said approving Jackdaw was “a serious misstep from the government” and sent the wrong signal about the UK’s climate commitments. She said ministers should instead focus on creating secure, well-paid jobs in the renewable sector for oil and gas workers and give similar support to the millions of employees in the public sector, which has also been hit by severe cuts in recent years.
“It’s time for the government to get its priorities straight: invest in clean energy, invest in the public services that communities rely on – to the benefit of us all.”
There is a split among the UK’s main trade unions on allowing fossil fuel companies to drill in the North Sea. Unite and GMB, which represent many oil and gas workers, back more licences, while Unison and the National Education Union oppose more drilling as part of a wider drive to create long term sustainable jobs and tackle the climate crisis.
One concern among unions is that jobs in the rapidly growing renewables sector are often not unionised and therefore not as secure or well paid as in those in the oil and gas sector.
However, last week Unison announced a new recognition deal with the UK’s largest energy company, Octopus Energy, known as a progressive organisation with a focus on renewable energy.
The GMB union had been attempting to gain recognition at Octopus but the company said Unison “stood out for its commitment to the energy transition”.
Egan said it was an important step to securing good, secure jobs in the renewable sector. “Unison is proud to be leading the way as the clean energy union. We urgently need more well-paid, unionised jobs and to transition away from fossil fuels at pace. This agreement is a step in the right direction on both counts.”

title: Poland: Protesters clash with police over sacked court chief
content_c:
Poland: Protesters clash with police over sacked court chief
October 31, 2026
Protesters gathered outside Poland's Constitutional Court on Friday night, with authorities sending police to the scene to secure the court's grounds.
It all comes after a statement appeared on the top court's website saying President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy had been suspended for one month. Fellow judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska will lead the institution during this period.
According to Warsaw police, officers responded to one judge who alerted them to possible threats to the safety of judges and staff.
Tusk vows to 'restore rule of law'
Swieczkowski is one of a slew of politically aligned judges who were appointed by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS), which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk backed the move in a post on X.
"Restoring the rule of law is our duty," Tusk said.
"After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way," he added.
When Tusk's center-left alliance took over after the 2023 parliamentary election, the group announced it would reverse controversial PiS government reforms in the judiciary.
Riot police deployed to court
Dozens of riot police were deployed to the court as followers of PiS protested against the ousting of Swieczkowski through the evening.
The court's official X social media account said there had been a "coup d'etat," with some chanting "Tusk traitor" as they condemned the step taken by the Tusk government.
Polish president cancels trip abroad
Right-wing Polish President Karol Nawrocki reacted to the situation by canceling a planned trip to Senegal.
"At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland," Nawrocki said.
Upon returning to Poland, he entered the Constitutional Court, making his way through the police barricade, his chief of staff said early on Saturday.
"President Karol Nawrocki, accompanied by the First President of the Supreme Court, Zbigniew Kapinski, entered the Constitutional Tribunal building," Pawel Szefernaker wrote on X.
In recent months, Nawrocki had refused to swear in five top court judges nominated by parliament.
When these judges instead took their oath before parliament, Swieczkowski had denied them access to the building.

title: Polen: Tumult und Protest vor dem Verfassungsgericht
content_c:
Polen Tumult und Protest vor dem Verfassungsgericht
Der Machtkampf um das polnische Verfassungsgericht spitzt sich zu. Die Polizei sicherte das Gebäude ab, nachdem sich Protestierende dort versammelt hatten. Auslöser ist die mutmaßliche Suspendierung der bisherigen Gerichtsführung.
In Polen ist ein Streit über das Verfassungsgericht eskaliert. Nach Angaben der Polizei sicherten Beamte das Gelände vor dem Gerichtshof, nachdem eine Richterin die Beamten wegen möglicher Gefahren für die Sicherheit von Richtern und Mitarbeitern alarmiert hatte.
Zuvor war auf der Internetseite des Verfassungsgerichts eine Mitteilung erschienen, wonach die Tätigkeit von Gerichtspräsident Bogdan Swieczkowski und seinem Stellvertreter für einen Monat ausgesetzt sei. In dieser Zeit werde die Verfassungsrichterin Anna Korwin-Piotrowska das Gericht führen. Kurz darauf erschien auf X ein Post des Verfassungsgerichts, der diese Information dementierte. Swieczkowski sei weiter im Amt. Korwin-Piotrowska könne ihn nicht vertreten, weil sie nicht vom Staatspräsidenten vereidigt worden sei. Das Gericht sprach von einem Staatsstreich.
Am Abend versammelten sich vor dem Gerichtsgebäude im Zentrum von Warschau viele Demonstranten, die meisten von ihnen Anhänger der oppositionellen PiS. Einige versuchten, Absperrungen zu durchbrechen und auf das Gelände vorzudringen. Nach Polizeiangaben wurden dabei drei Menschen festgenommen. Viele Demonstranten harrten auch am späten Abend noch vor dem Gerichtshof aus.
Nawrocki bricht Staatsbesuch ab
Der rechtskonservative Präsident Nawrocki brach seine geplante Reise in den Senegal ab. "In einem solchen Moment muss der Präsident in Polen sein", schrieb Nawrocki auf der Plattform X. Sein Flugzeug landete am Abend wieder in Warschau. Später traf er am Gericht ein.
Auf einem Video, das der von Tusks Regierung neu nominierte Verfassungsrichter Maciej Berek auf X veröffentlichte, ist zu sehen, wie sich der ehemalige Amateurboxer Nawrocki mit robustem Körpereinsatz in das Gerichtsgebäude drängt. Nachdem nach der Parlamentswahl 2023 Tusks Mitte-Links-Bündnis die Regierung übernommen hatte, kündigte sie an, die Neuerungen der PiS-Regierung im Justizwesen rückgängig zu machen. Zu den neu nominierten Verfassungsrichtern, die Nawrocki nicht vereidigen wollte, zählte auch die Juristin Anna Korwin-Piotrowska. Als Dienstälteste habe sie daher für den 3. November eine Sitzung aller Verfassungsrichter einberufen.
Tusk spricht von Wiederherstellung des Rechtsstaats
Regierungschef Donald Tusk betonte auf X, die Wiederherstellung der Rechtsstaatlichkeit sei eine Verpflichtung für seine Regierung. "Nach Jahren der Rechtslosigkeit unter der PiS-Regierung ist dies ein schwieriger, manchmal schmerzhafter Prozess, der entschlossenes Handeln erfordert. Es gibt keinen anderen Weg."
Justizminister Waldemar Zurek beantragte die Aufhebung der Immunität Swieczkowskis und seines Stellvertreters. "Dieses Gericht ist zu Privateigentum geworden. Wir müssen dafür sorgen, dass es wieder ordnungsgemäß funktioniert", sagte er.

title: Behörden in Israel weisen Wahlbetrugsvorwürfe zurück
content_c:
Behörden in Israel weisen Wahlbetrugsvorwürfe zurück
30. Oktober 2026
Ausländische Akteure sollen möglicherweise versucht haben, die Wählermobilisierung in arabischen Gemeinden während der Parlamentswahlen dieser Woche zu beeinflussen. Das zumindest behauptete die Partei des israelischen Ministerpräsidenten Benjamin Netanjahu, Likud, am Donnerstagmorgen.
No'am Sohlberg, Richter am Obersten Gerichtshof und Vorsitzender der Zentralen Wahlkommission, forderte den Inlandsgeheimdienst Schin Bet in einem Brief auf, die Vorwürfe von Likud näher zu untersuchen.
Laut Erklärung des Likud hätten die arabischen Parteien Ra'am und die Vereinigte Arabische Liste "schwere Straftaten" begangen, um die Wähler und Wählerinnen an die Wahlurnen zu treiben, unter anderem mit Bestechung, Drohungen und anderen Formen des Wahlbetrugs. Die Parteien hatten am Dienstag einen Rekordanteil an den abgegebenen Stimmen erzielt, was vor allem auf die ungewöhnlich hohe Wahlbeteiligung in Gemeinden mit arabischen und palästinensischen Bürgern mit israelischer Staatsangehörigkeit zurückzuführen ist.
"Mir wurden schwerwiegende Verdachtsmomente zur Kenntnis gebracht, die eine unzulässige Einmischung in die Wahlen in Form von Finanzmitteln aus dem Ausland durch externe Akteure, die gegen die Interessen Israels handeln, betreffen", schreibt Sohlberg in seinem Brief. Er selbst sei nicht in der Lage, zu bestätigen, dass die Anschuldigungen wahr seien, fügt er hinzu.
"Die Wahlen in Israel wurden gestohlen von arabischen Parteien, die den Terrorismus und die Auslöschung des israelischen Staates unterstützen", erklärte der Likud in seiner Stellungnahme. Die Partei von Ministerpräsident Benjamin Netanjahu und seine Regierungskoalition haben bei der Wahl Sitze verloren, so dass weder sie noch ihre Gegner über ein Mehrheit im Parlament verfügen, es sei denn, sie arbeiten mit einer oder beiden arabischen Parteien zusammen.
Als Begründung für die Forderung nach einer Untersuchung verweisen der Likud ebenso wie andere Vertreter des rechten Lagers auf die ungewöhnlich hohe Wahlbeteiligung in arabischen Gemeinden, Berichte über organisierte Fahrten zu den Wahllokalen und Bedenken hinsichtlich von ausländischen Akteuren finanzierter Kampagnen zur Wählermobilisierung. Eine formale Überprüfung sei erforderlich, um das öffentliche Vertrauen in den Wahlprozess zu erhalten, unabhängig davon, ob letztlich ein Fehlverhalten festgestellt würde.
Behörden weisen Vorwürfe zurück
Durchgeführt werden die Wahlen in Israel von der Zentralen Wahlkommission. Diese setzt sich aus Repräsentanten der im Parlament vertretenen Parteien zusammen, den Vorsitz führt ein Richter des Obersten Gerichtshofs. Wahlbetrug in großem Stil war in der Vergangenheit selten, doch Streitigkeiten über den Ablauf des Wahlkampfs und die Abstimmungsverfahren gibt es regelmäßig.
Der israelischen Polizei zufolge gibt es keine Beweise für die Behauptung des Likud, weder "ermittlungsbezogene" noch "informative". "Am Wahltag kam es nur zu geringfügigen Irregularitäten hinsichtlich der Integrität der Wahlen, auch im Vergleich zu früheren Wahlen", stellte die Polizei in einer Erklärung fest.
Auch ein hochrangiger Vertreter der Zentralen Wahlkommission wies die Vorwürfe zurück. "Es gibt keine Basis für die Behauptung von 'gestohlenen Wahlen'", sagte Dean Livne, amtierender Leiter der Kommission im Gespräch mit dem israelischen Sender Kan 11. Bei der Kommission gingen "Behauptungen anstelle von Beweisen" des Likud und anderen Parteien ein.
Andere Parteien unterstützen eine Untersuchung
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanjahus wichtigster Herausforderer und Vorsitzender der Partei Jaschar, warf dem israelischen Ministerpräsidenten vor, eine "unlautere Einflusskampagne" zu führen, um Zweifel an den Wahlen zu säen und eine "fiktive Delegitimierung" des künftigen Parlaments zu betreiben. Er forderte aber ebenfalls, die Wahlbetrugsvorwürfe des Likud zu untersuchen.
Die religiöse muslimische Partei Ra'am wies Vorwürfe einer Beteiligung an Wahlbetrug zurück und erklärte sich bereit, bei allen Ermittlungen zu kooperieren.
Katar veröffentlichte eine Erklärung, in der es jede Beteiligung an den israelischen Wahlen dementierte. Es handle sich um "falsche Propaganda, die darauf abzielt, Katars Namen in Israels politische Konflikte hineinzuziehen", heißt es in der Erklärung.
Die Auseinandersetzung fällt in eine Zeit, in der die israelische Politik immer polarisierter wird und das Misstrauen zwischen den rivalisierenden politischen Lagern wächst.
Ziel des Likud könnte es sein, den Einfluss arabischer Akteure auf die israelische Politik zu verringern, sagt Amira Halperin vom Palm Beach Center for Democracy and Policy Research. "Die Stimmen der arabischen Wähler haben bei diesen Wahlen eine sehr, sehr große Rolle gespielt", meint sie.
Die Vorwürfe könnten das Vertrauen der Öffentlichkeit in den Wahlprozess beschädigen, fürchtet Halperin. "Mit Aussagen bezüglich eines Scheiterns des demokratischen Systems sollten wir uns zurückhalten."
Ermittlungen des Schin Bet
Berichten israelischer Medien zufolge basieren einige der vom Likud genannten Bedenken auf Geheimdienstanalysen, die vom Schin Bet geprüft worden waren. Öffentlich bestätigt hat der Dienst Einzelheiten solcher Erkenntnisse jedoch nicht.
Das Ausmaß der Verdachtsmomente sei "relativ gering", berichtete der öffentlich-rechtliche Sender Kan unter Berufung auf Quellen, die mit den Ermittlungen des Schin Bet vertraut sind. Die Tageszeitung "Ha'aretz" zitierte ebenfalls Quellen, die mit den Vorwürfen vertraut sind und die Berichte als "überzogen" bezeichneten.
David Zini, der Leiter des Inlandsgeheimdienstes, bezeichnete die Wahlen in Israel am Wahltag als "sicher, reibungslos und unter Kontrolle" und fügte hinzu, die Wahlkommission und die israelische Polizei würden "erfolgreich" verhindern, dass jemand den Wahlprozess in den Wahlprozess eingreife.
Zinis Ernennung vor einem Jahr war von Vertretern der Opposition kritisiert worden. Sie stellten sowohl seine Eignung als auch die Motive Netanjahus für die Ernennung in Frage. Befürworter dagegen argumentierten, Zini sei aufgrund seiner militärischen Erfahrung und seines sicherheitspolitischen Hintergrunds für das Amt geeignet.
Unabhängig davon hat der Inlandsgeheimdienst gegen mehrere der engsten Vertrauten Netanjahus wegen des Vorwurfs verdeckter Verbindungen zu Katar ermittelt. Sie stehen jedoch in keinem Zusammenhang mit den aktuellen Vorwürfen des Wahlbetrugs.
Im Vorfeld geplant?
Wie die israelische Plattform N12 berichtete, sprachen Vertreter des Likud am Wochenende vor den Wahlen darüber, welche Beschwerden über die Integrität der Wahlen schon im Vorfeld der Wahlen erhoben werden könnten, mit Schwerpunkt auf arabischen und palästinensischen Gemeinden. Beweise über tatsächliche Unregelmäßigkeiten lagen zu diesem Zeitpunkt allerdings keine vor.
"Sie setzten sich zusammen und suchten gemeinsam nach kreativen Ideen, um sich zu beschweren", sagte Daphna Liel, die Journalistin, die darüber berichtete.
Hohe Wahlbeteiligung
Die Wahlbeteiligung arabischer und palästinensischer Wähler erreichte bei diesen Wahlen einen historischen Rekord. Während sie 2022 bei etwa 50 Prozent lag, gaben laut Berichten aus Israel in diesem Jahr etwa 80 Prozent ihre Stimme ab.
In den vergangenen Jahrzehnten war die Wahlbeteiligung der arabischen Bevölkerung großen Schwankungen unterlegen. Beeinflusst wurde die Beteiligung häufig durch Diskussionen innerhalb der arabischen Gesellschaft darüber, welche Rolle die Teilnahme an nationalen Wahlen dabei spielen kann. Werden die Interessen der arabischen Bürger und Bürgerinnen, die lediglich etwa 20 Prozent der israelischen Bevölkerung ausmachen, dadurch vorangebracht? Die außergewöhnlich hohe Beteiligung in diesem Jahr wird von vielen als Zeichen einer neuen politischen Mobilisierung gesehen.
Für die Vereinigte Liste und Ra'am führte das zu einem großen Erfolg. Sie gewannen je elf und acht Sitze im neuen Parlament. 2022 waren es lediglich sechs und vier. Beide Parteien haben sich bereits bereit erklärt, mit Israels zionistischer Opposition zusammenzuarbeiten, um Netanjahu aus dem Amt zu drängen.
Vor den Wahlen hatte die Mehrzahl der zur zionistischen Opposition zählenden Parteien versprochen, keine Koalition mit arabischen Parteien einzugehen. Einzige Ausnahme war hier die sozialdemokratische zionistische Partei HaDemocratim (Demokratische Partei).
Am Wahltag selbst wurden Vorwürfe laut, dass es in arabischen und palästinensischen Wahllokalen zu "systematischen Verzögerungen" käme, wie Adalah, eine israelisch-palästinensische Nicht-Regierungsorganisation, die sich für die Rechte der arabischen Minderheit in Israel einsetzt, berichtete.
Adaptiert aus dem Englischen von Phoenix Hanzo.
description: Bei den Wahlen in Israel habe es eine groß angelegte Einmischung durch das Ausland gegeben, behauptet die Partei von Ministerpräsident Benjamin Netanjahu. Im Zentrum der Vorwürfe stehen die arabischen Parteien.

Die Wahlbeteiligung arabischer und palästinensischer Wähler erreichte bei diesen Wahlen einen historischen Rekord. Während sie 2022 bei etwa 50 Prozent lag, gaben laut Berichten aus Israel in diesem Jahr etwa 80 Prozent ihre Stimme ab.
In den vergangenen Jahrzehnten war die Wahlbeteiligung der arabischen Bevölkerung großen Schwankungen unterlegen. Beeinflusst wurde die Beteiligung häufig durch Diskussionen innerhalb der arabischen Gesellschaft darüber, welche Rolle die Teilnahme an nationalen Wahlen dabei spielen kann. Werden die Interessen der arabischen Bürger und Bürgerinnen, die lediglich etwa 20 Prozent der israelischen Bevölkerung ausmachen, dadurch vorangebracht? Die außergewöhnlich hohe Beteiligung in diesem Jahr wird von vielen als Zeichen einer neuen politischen Mobilisierung gesehen.
Für die Vereinigte Liste und Ra'am führte das zu einem großen Erfolg. Sie gewannen je elf und acht Sitze im neuen Parlament. 2022 waren es lediglich sechs und vier. Beide Parteien haben sich bereits bereit erklärt, mit Israels zionistischer Opposition zusammenzuarbeiten, um Netanjahu aus dem Amt zu drängen.
Vor den Wahlen hatte die Mehrzahl der zur zionistischen Opposition zählenden Parteien versprochen, keine Koalition mit arabischen Parteien einzugehen. Einzige Ausnahme war hier die sozialdemokratische zionistische Partei HaDemocratim (Demokratische Partei).
Am Wahltag selbst wurden Vorwürfe laut, dass es in arabischen und palästinensischen Wahllokalen zu "systematischen Verzögerungen" käme, wie Adalah, eine israelisch-palästinensische Nicht-Regierungsorganisation, die sich für die Rechte der arabischen Minderheit in Israel einsetzt, berichtete.
Adaptiert aus dem Englischen von Phoenix Hanzo.

title: Очільник МЗС Британії жорстко звернувся до Лаврова на G20: просто в обличчя нагадав про вбитих українців
content_c:
Очільник МЗС Британії жорстко звернувся до Лаврова на G20: просто в обличчя нагадав про вбитих українців
Британський міністр поставив Лаврова перед фактом: згадав убитих у Дніпрі та звернувся до Путіна.
Очільник МЗС Великої Британії Ед Мілібенд жорстко розніс російського колегу Сергія Лаврова: нагадав про вбитих українців і прямо назвав Росію агресором.
Про це він заявив під час зустрічі міністрів закордонних справ G20, повідомляє Sky News.
Мілібенд нагадав про загибель мирних жителів в Україні та наголосив, що Росія не перемагає у війні завдяки мужності українців і підтримці союзників.
«Давайте поговоримо про те, що сталося вчора на залізниці у Дніпрі. Лише вчора ваші дрони атакували та вбили 15 людей», — звернувся британський міністр до Лаврова.
Він додав, що це лише один із прикладів убивств мирних жителів за майже п’ять років повномасштабного вторгнення. Британський політик закликав тиснути на Москву і позбавляти диктатора Володимира Путіна доходів, які дають змогу продовжувати «цю варварську війну».
«Путін тоді думав, що легко переможе у цій війні. Але ви не перемагаєте. Завдяки мужності українського народу та солідарності країн за цим столом ви не перемагаєте», — заявив Мілібенд.
Він також закликав Лаврова набратися сміливості та сказати правду російському диктаторові.
«Якби у вас вистачило сміливості говорити правду і чинити правильно, ви сказали б Путіну, що він не перемагає у цій війні й не переможе», — наголосив очільник британського МЗС.
Окремо Мілібенд Ця заява пролунала на тлі нещодавнього блокування Дональдом Трампом санкцій проти Кремля.
Звинувачення Каллас
Водночас висока представниця ЄС із закордонних справ Кая Каллас звинуватила Лаврова у поширенні брехні про війну і охарактеризував поведінку російського міністра на засіданні як «доволі провокативну».
«Звісно, він навів чимало брехні та перекрутив факти, які ми згодом змогли спростувати», — заявила Каллас, повідомило видання Der Stern.
За її словами, Лавров під час зустрічі не продемонстрував жодних ознак готовності Москви до мирних переговорів. Зокрема, свідченням цього є смертельні атаки РФ по Україні.
Каллас також закликала посилити тиск на Крнмля, зокрема задля досягнення припинення вогню в Чорному морі.
«Для нас цілком очевидно: щоб покласти край цій війні, тиск потрібно чинити на агресора», — підсумувала вона.
Скандал із Лавровим на саміті G20
Перед початком саміту організатори скасували заплановану спільну фотосесію. Причиною стала відмова Мілібенда і інших європейських лідерів фотографуватися поруч із Лавровим.
Сам Лавров згодом іронічно прокоментував цей епізод,
«Якщо для них найважливіше — як вони виглядають на спільному фото і хто стоїть поруч, то це саме за себе говорить», — заявив російський міністр, назвавши епізод «дипломатією сімейного фото».
Зауважимо, що Лавров летів до Атланти у США понад 20 годин через обхід так званих «недружніх країн», які закрили свій повітряний простір для російських бортів. Візит очільника МЗС РФ відбувається попри спротив частини американських законодавців, які закликали не впускати політика країни-агресора до Штатів.

title: У подножья подводной горы в Австралии собралось 2,8 миллиона угрей: почему
content_c:
Ученые под руководством морского биолога Бена Скулдинга из австралийской организации CSIRO впервые оценили, сколько угрей собирается у подводной горы Пейшенс недалеко от Тасмании. По их оценкам, сюда приплывает 2,8 миллиона угрей, общая масса которых превышает 3500 метрических тонн, сообщает Science Alert.
Миллионы угрей собираются у подножья подводной горы каждый год. Они приплывают сюда для размножения. Но вопрос о том, почему угри выбирают именно этот регион, оставался открытым.
«Это один из самых важных вопросов, на него пока нет ответа. Подводная гора Пейшенс — одна из примерно 120 подобных гор в морских парках Хьюон и Тасман-Фракчер к югу от Тасмании. И хотя расположенные поблизости подводные горы имеют схожую глубину и общие природные характеристики, на них не наблюдается такого же скопления угрей. На данном этапе у нас есть несколько обоснованных гипотез, но окончательного ответа пока нет», — сказал Скулдинг.
Чтобы определить истинный масштаб ежегодных скоплений угрей-корзиночников возле горы ученым потребовались десятки лет исследований. О необычно большом количестве этих угрей в данном районе сообщали представители коммерческого рыболовства — еще в 1980-х и 1990-х годах, но снять на видео такие скопления удалось только в 2007 году.
Последующие исследования позволили узнать больше. Угри обитают на подводной горе круглый год, но их численность достигает пика осенью в Южном полушарии – с марта по май. Угри, которых поймали в это время, оказались в состоянии готовности к нересту. Это указало на то, что они действительно собираются здесь для размножения.
В статье 2021 года, посвященной этому скоплению, на основе гидроакустических измерений и подсчета угрей по видеозаписям было сделано предположение, что в апреле 2015 года в месте скопления могло находиться несколько десятков тысяч угрей. Но Скулдинг и его коллеги хотели однозначно ответить на этот вопрос.
В период с 2023 по 2025 год исследователи провели серию съемок в районе подводной горы Пейшенс, используя гидролокаторы для картирования огромных скоплений рыбы. Но возникла проблема: здесь собирались не только угри, а различить виды рыб с помощью эхолокатора нельзя.
Поэтому ученые сопоставили данные акустических измерений с материалами подводной видеосъемки, что позволило определить, какой вклад каждый из видов вносит в общий сигнал гидролокатора. В результате ученые выявили, что в пиковые периоды скопление достигает трех километров в длину, двух – в ширину и примерно 150 метров в высоту над морским дном.
По оценкам исследователей, биомасса угрей увеличилась примерно с 750 метрических тонн в марте до более 3500 метрических тонн в мае.
Ранее ученые заметили новый необычный тип охоты у косаток. Они атаковали рыбу-солнце и разрывали ее на части.

title: "Прокинулася розгубленою і з болем". Перша заява Крісти Пайк після невдалої страти
content_c:
"Прокинулася розгубленою і з болем". Перша заява Крісти Пайк після невдалої страти
Кріста Пайк, засуджена до смертної кари у США, оприлюднила свою першу публічну заяву після невдалої спроби страти у вересні.
"Від тієї ночі не було жодної миті, коли б я не відчувала болю", - йдеться в заяві, яку її юридична команда опублікувала в соціальних мережах у п'ятницю.
"У мене болить тіло. Болять руки. Болять кисті. Болить горло. Мені й досі важко говорити. І біль не лише фізичний. Він є в моїй свідомості й душі", - каже Пайк.
50-річну Пайк виписали з лікарні наприкінці минулого місяця. Вона вижила після двох ін'єкцій смертельної дози препарату пентобарбітал, які призвели до її критичного стану.
Після цього її повернули до в'язниці, де вона провела останні 30 років за вбивство Коллін Слеммер у 1995 році.
Вважають, що Пайк - єдина людина, яка пережила спробу страти за допомогою смертельної ін'єкції.
Раніше її адвокати повідомляли, що після невдалої спроби страти вона захворіла на пневмонію, її руки сильно набрякли, а також вона не могла ковтати.
"Я одужую і знаю, що стаю сильнішою, - сказала вона у своїй заяві в п'ятницю. - Але одужання не означає, що зі мною вже все гаразд".

content:

title: Spain train disaster clouds Sánchez chances of re-election
content_c:
Spain train disaster clouds Sánchez chances of re-election
- Published
The breaking news from Spain this week was shocking but also shockingly familiar: another collision on the high-speed rail line south from Madrid, with reports of dozens killed.
It is just nine months since two trains crashed near Cordoba, killing 46 people. Now 69 bodies have been recovered here in central Spain, from wreckage strewn over the tracks and down an embankment.
For the victims' families it is devastating; a personal tragedy.
But it is also a national disaster that has shattered confidence in the country's rail network and the Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez. It is playing out just weeks before the snap general election he called.
The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative.
From the first hours after the collision, Transport Minister Oscar Puente began suggesting "human error" was to blame, batting responsibility as far as possible from the cabinet.
On Friday, he appeared before the press for a second time to set out what he called the "objective facts" of the crash and counter a surge of criticism against the government.
The opposition People's Party (PP) is among those calling for his resignation as a "moral" and "ethical" move.
Instead after expressing "huge pain and sadness" for the victims, Puente went on the offensive.
He rejected talk of chronic underinvestment in infrastructure and insisted that Spain's high-speed signalling safety system, the LZB, was neither old nor inadequate: Germany and Austria use the same.
In Spain, it has already failed 170 times so far this year, he revealed, but called that "normal" and around the EU average.
The problem surrounds what happens next - when the system fails and control of the line shifts to manual.
In this case, the minister highlighted a series of human errors that proved catastrophic.
Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.
The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid.
"They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop.
"I'm no judge... But these are the facts."
So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister.
"I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."
But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading.
"This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.
An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz, near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails - very different to the latest collision.
But there is a similar impact.
"It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."
For Team Sánchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.
Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.
Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.
Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.
That's when Sánchez called an early election.
His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.
Most recent polls showed the centre-right PP coming first and forming a coalition with the far-right Vox.
"They have this majority in almost 95% of the simulations we have done," Prof Pablo Simon of Madrid's Carlos III University explains.
But Sánchez had been running a positive campaign, trying to lure apathetic voters to the polls to vote socialist.
Suddenly, the tone has changed.
"They've totally lost control of the agenda and the emotion of this campaign," Simon says. "It's going to be extremely difficult now. There is this general mood of decay, of a country that's not working properly. A depression."
There is also anger.
There have already been small protests over the train crash led by far-right groups in Madrid and large numbers of police are on stand-by this weekend ahead of further potential clashes, organised online.
Here in Toledo, the mood is nervous.
"We all travelled in silence and really sad," Paloma told me at the city station, where she had just pulled in on a half empty train.
She admitted she's scared of the high-speed network now and angry at the government.
"This crash will change all of our votes, completely," Paloma said. "We'll shift from the left wing to the right. Because of everything that's happened."
Lucia takes the high-speed AVE into Madrid each day, and is scared too.
"This was human error. But there's been two accidents now with more than 100 dead," she says. "Things here are really bad. They have to change."
Producer Davide Ghiglione contributed to this report

title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
content_c:
Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
- Published
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.
The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.
It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.
Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.
The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.
Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.
While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.
Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather than announced in the Budget.
He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".
Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".
Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.
"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."
He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments to cut their capital budgets by 1%.
Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.
"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."
Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".
He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".
He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".
"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.
Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and the Nato-wide target of 3.5% by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.
Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".
Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.
In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.
But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".
"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.

title: Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales
content_c:
Google value plunges by $500bn as its own AI search hits ad sales
- Published
Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hitting search advertising revenue.
Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said Google's "AI mode", where it answers questions conversationally, was eating into the money it makes from ads which appear next to results to traditional search questions.
Yet, Schindler said he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine.
Google's role in answering the world's questions has been challenged by the AI boom, with millions of people using programs such as ChatGPT and Claude instead.
Kim Scott, who formerly led Google's advertising business, told the BBC's Today programme that the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch" by having its own AI summaries hit its search revenue.
She said that Google was founded on the idea of making long-term bets on technology – even if they hurt the firm in the short term.
"I think they're making a long-term bet on AI," she said.
In its results published on Wednesday, Alphabet revealed that total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn.
However, the firm did not make as much money as analysts had predicted, particularly in its advertising arm, which spooked many investors.
Shares in the company plummeted over 12% to a six-month low following the release of the results.
By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.
Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing Search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."
Investors not buying Amazon's trillion-dollar business hopes
Microsoft and Amazon also issued updates this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending huge sums of cash in the ongoing AI race.
But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.
Amazon's stock took a hit on Thursday , with its shares falling 6% in after-hours trading.
Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.
That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.
Jassy noted that Amazon's cloud services business, as well as retail stores, may be those businesses. During a call with financial analysts he also repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.
"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."
As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.
"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
Microsoft begs the question of AI's real value
Wall Street's reaction to Microsoft's update was more muted, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.
The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.
Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.
Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.
Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.
But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI.
"Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

Google-owner Alphabet lost just over $500bn (£374bn) in value on Thursday after it revealed its own artificial intelligence (AI) summaries were hitting search advertising revenue.
Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said Google's "AI mode", where it answers questions conversationally, was eating into the money it makes from ads which appear next to results to traditional search questions.
Yet, Schindler said he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine.
Google's role in answering the world's questions has been challenged by the AI boom, with millions of people using programs such as ChatGPT and Claude instead.
Kim Scott, who formerly led Google's advertising business, told the BBC's Today programme that the company would "rather eat its own lunch than allow someone else to eat their lunch" by having its own AI summaries hit its search revenue.
She said that Google was founded on the idea of making long-term bets on technology – even if they hurt the firm in the short term.
"I think they're making a long-term bet on AI," she said.
In its results published on Wednesday, Alphabet revealed that total revenue grew 25% in the three months to the end of September, compared to the same period last year, hitting $127.6bn.
However, the firm did not make as much money as analysts had predicted, particularly in its advertising arm, which spooked many investors.
Shares in the company plummeted over 12% to a six-month low following the release of the results.
By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.
Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing Search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."
Investors not buying Amazon's trillion-dollar business hopes
Microsoft and Amazon also issued updates this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending huge sums of cash in the ongoing AI race.
But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.
Amazon's stock took a hit on Thursday , with its shares falling 6% in after-hours trading.
Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.
That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.
Jassy noted that Amazon's cloud services business, as well as retail stores, may be those businesses. During a call with financial analysts he also repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.
"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."
As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.
"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
Microsoft begs the question of AI's real value
Wall Street's reaction to Microsoft's update was more muted, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.
The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.
Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.
Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.
Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.
But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI.
"Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

title: Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
content_c:
Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.
In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.
Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.
The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.
Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.
Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.
“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.
In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.
Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

title: Healey’s budget cuts mean Britain is likely to miss green heating targets
content_c:
Britain is unlikely to hit its targets on green heating after the cuts announced by John Healey this week, experts have warned, as critics of Ed Miliband claim the former energy secretary’s green agenda is being dismantled.
The chancellor unveiled more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department’s budget this week, much of which will pay for higher defence spending.
One casualty of the cuts is the government’s scheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions are being undermined.
Some believe the cuts are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh. However, energy department sources insisted the government’s longer-term changes will incentivise people to move towards cleaner power sources and benefit the overall green agenda.
Andrew Sissons, a director at the research charity Nesta, said: “After the cuts announced on Wednesday, it is very difficult to see how we can hit our clean heating targets. It is even possible that a Labour government will be the first to miss the targets it has signed up to in the current carbon budget.”
Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments.
Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.
Under the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, and was planning to increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30.
The plan forms a key part of the UK’s programme to clean up its heating networks and hit its overall emissions reduction targets. However, ministers said on Wednesday the scheme’s funding would rise only in line with inflation, meaning the number of installations is likely to stagnate or rise much more slowly than previously planned.
“It’s disappointing – so frustrating,” said Ed Matthew, the director of the UK programme at the thinktank E3G. “We are behind a lot of other countries in rolling out heat pumps and we need a sea change in take-up to change that.”
The cuts to heat pump subsidies came alongside about £250m of other cuts to the warm homes plan, £500m worth of cuts to hydrogen schemes, and £200m to funding for carbon capture and storage technology – all projects once championed by Miliband.
Healey also announced that renewable projects would only be approved in future if they could be shown to bring costs down and were ready to be connected with the grid. Officials insist the government remains committed to its target of having clean power by 2030, though many experts believe that will be impossible under the new system.
One government source said: “This is probably the most significant shift we have seen in energy policy since we came to office. The emphasis now is on cost, not just building to make sure there is enough capacity to hit our green targets.”
Paul Ovenden, a former adviser to Keir Starmer, said: “It is fascinating to see the energy capital budgets being raided to fund defence – this is the bones of Ed Miliband’s project being picked clean.
“This was something that has been discussed in government before – but Miliband always won that argument. Now he’s not in that department any more, it’s happened.”
Ovenden added: “Had he not helped to oust Starmer and Reeves, he’d probably be in post still and it wouldn’t have been possible.”
But allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever. They pointed out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed.
They also said the government’s intention to change energy markets so electricity prices are no longer so attached to gas prices would help encourage consumers to move away from fossil fuels.
One source said: “Ed and Miatta have both made affordability their focus. It would be wrong to suggest that prioritising cost is in any way a shift away from the green agenda.”
A spokesperson for the energy department said: “Over the last two years, we have made considerable progress, thanks to the momentum of clean power 2030, seeing £110bn of private-sector investment announced and securing enough clean power for over 20m homes.
“We are committed to making the most of clean, homegrown power and meeting our heat pump target to protect consumers from volatile fossil fuel prices.”
