author: Josh Butler
content:
Altering copyright law to allow AI companies to scrape music, books and journalism could trigger a constitutional breach, Coalition senators and the recording industry have warned, as they raise new fears it could open Australia to massive legal action and compensation claims from rights holders worldwide.
The attorney general’s department admitted it was “extremely alive” to the issue, and Australia’s leading constitutional expert, Anne Twomey, agreed there was “potentially” a concern – depending how legislation was drafted – that granting AI companies permission to scrape copyrighted material from the internet could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.
In a simmering debate centred on the same legal point as the movie The Castle, the question of acquiring property “on just terms” is emerging as a key concern amid furious lobbying from tech companies and rights holders ahead of a looming federal government announcement on AI.
“We could be liable for ‘just terms’ compensation for acquiring that property for every rights holder on Earth,” Ross Cadell, a Nationals senator, told Guardian Australia.
Michaelia Cash, the shadow attorney general, said the government should not “sell out Australian creators and rights holders in the rush to entice AI investment”.
Labor is mulling copyright changes in a suite of reforms around AI, including datacentres, online safety, workforce, energy and the economy. While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train on Australian material.
Some AI companies have rejected making licensing agreements under existing copyright law, saying it was too difficult. Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder deployed digital protections signaling an objection.
A fresh concern being aired by sceptics and creatives is that any weakening of copyright to benefit AI could represent a breach of section 51 of the constitution, which allows the commonwealth to make laws about “the acquisition of property on just terms”.
“If they go ahead with an opt-out model, it does raise a real question of whether the government is acquiring the intellectual property rights of others,” said Cadell, a member of the federal parliamentary committee on AI.
“How we support property rights is core to this.”
A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives and pledged that “any future copyright changes deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.
Anne Twomey, professor emerita of law at the University of Sydney, said the issue was exceedingly complex and noted no legislative proposal had been aired. She said numerous cases had come before the high court relating to copyright and acquisition of property, including about video games, cigarette plain packaging and cassette tapes, with varying outcomes.
Twomey expected the federal government would be hyperaware of such concerns, but said granting a new right to AI companies to use copyrighted material and diminishing the rights of copyright holders could “potentially” trigger constitutional issues.
“The high court has recognised a number of exceptions to section 51 … One would want to be quite confident before enacting the legislation about whether or not section 51 would apply,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.
She said any change allowing Australia to host AI companies training on international data could potentially create grounds for global rights holders to take legal action here.
Cadell told Guardian Australia he worried about such a development opening the federal government to liability for “the biggest compensation rights case in history”.
Cadell raised his concerns about the constitution in a committee hearing with the attorney general’s department on Friday, in which officials said they were conscious of those issues.
Officials did not directly answer when Cadell asked about international implications and liability for compensation to foreign rights holders.
Annabelle Herd, the CEO of the Australian Recording Industry Association, claimed any proposal to allow AI companies to scrape data was “clearly an acquisition of property”.
“It’s hard to imagine what kind of compensation would make up for the fact that they’re basically taking our right … and trading it away to the AI companies to then monetise themselves, and that appears to be a clear path to a constitutional challenge.”
Chris Maund, CEO of Mushroom Records, said current copyright law was working and that AI companies should use existing licensing arrangements, noting companies such as Spotify were already making AI-related deals.
He also raised concern about international ramifications were Australia to change copyright law, saying it would not only apply to Australian artists and copyright owners.
“The AI company could do their training here in Australia and circumvent the copyright laws that apply outside of Australia, and that’s why the international creative industries are watching this very closely,” he said.
Maund said international rights holder groups had been urging Labor not to weaken copyright law. Guardian Australia has provided submissions to the Joint Select Committee as a member of Australia’s wider rights holder community.
“The Australian government has been really great to the music industry, particularly Prime Minister Albanese and Tony Burke. They’ve set up Creative Music Australia, which companies like us and our artists have done very well out of, but it feels like they’re out of step with artists and copyright owners on this point,” he said.
Cash said the Coalition welcomed the benefits of AI and wanted investment, but also raised the constitutional concern.
“That is the prime minister’s own test, and the government should be held to it,” she said of compensation to rights holders.
“The constitutional question of property rights and their acquisition on just terms is also a live issue we will be examining depending on what the government puts forward.”
Cadell said while AI had benefits, he worried about its risks.
“There’s lots of talk about what the benefits may be and what may happen. But if we take these rights away, we know what will happen,” Cadell said.
“I don’t want to hurt people for a ‘may’.”

title: How do you bounce back from Liz Truss-level public failure? Don’t be shameless; do show remorse | Gaby Hinsliff
content_c:
Gabriel Weston made a mistake at work this summer. It doesn’t define her – she was and is a well-regarded NHS surgeon and author – but it was serious enough, as she explained in an extraordinarily candid series of Instagram and Substack posts this month, to prompt an investigation that left her feeling “ashamed and alone and really quite nervous”. Whatever went wrong in the operating theatre was bad enough to be classed a “never event” (something that should never be able to happen if the process is working properly) and triggered a nagging anxiety that she might somehow do it again, unless she figured out where she had unexpectedly gone wrong.
It’s a fascinating insight into a process that most people never have the courage to talk about openly. But it also highlights why it’s so hard in practice for doctors and other professionals to acknowledge and learn from mistakes – as every public inquiry into every public scandal ends up recommending, only to repeat it all over again after the next one – rather than close ranks and cover up. Weston says she only spoke up out of frustration with what she saw as her employers’ failure to support her (she had asked to reduce what she considered an overloaded operating list to take some pressure off, which she says has now happened, leaving her full of praise for the hospital’s ultimate response). Judging by the responses to her posts, she’s not alone.
I thought of Weston this week when Liz Truss published Bank Job, the second book she has written in two years circling the drain of her career. This one seems if anything even less self-aware, blaming the Bank of England, not herself, for the spectacular failure of her mini-budget (even her old cheerleaders at the Telegraph called it deranged). But it’s also oddly sad. There’s something near-pathological about the inability to engage with an excruciatingly public failure, as if the truth would shatter her. She can’t seem to leave the whole episode alone – can’t withdraw, as Keir Starmer has, into stony silence about his own prematurely curtailed time in Downing Street – yet can’t really face it head-on either.
How does anyone learn from cataclysmic failure? I don’t mean the frothy, early-career kind that seemed the end of the world at the time, but which you can laugh about now from the security of knowing that eventually everything turned out fine. Those aren’t the kind of failures the state really cares about avoiding. Nor do I mean the kind whose authors somehow manage to fail upwards anyway – or at least onwards, like Truss, into some strange reincarnation on YouTube. The failures that most haunt their authors, but which often hold the most useful lessons for preventing such a thing ever happening again, are often of the “there but for the grace of God go you and I” kind, involving formerly blameless and conscientious people who make one inexplicably dumb mistake, often under pressure or when exhausted.
Richard Jackson was a high-flying civil servant working on counter-terrorism, who one night accidentally scooped up two classified documents that should never have left the building along with some routine papers he was taking home. Realising his error that night, he fatally compounded it by deciding to sneak the files back before their absence was noticed, only to accidentally leave them on the train – where they were found and handed into a BBC reporter, resulting in a security scandal that cost Jackson his job and left him close to suicide. The advice on coping he shared in a recent episode of BBC Radio 4’s Life Changing series – get dark thoughts out of your head by writing them down or telling someone; keep a note of all the nice things people have ever said to you; don’t let your life be defined by one mistake – seems useful for individuals in the eye of the storm. But so perhaps is what Weston calls a degree of professional “care and acceptance” for good people who have failed, and want help working out why.
Shamelessness has a deservedly terrible reputation in public life, and for some mistakes forgiveness can be too much to ask.
But it’s shame that prevents thoughtful people learning from failure; shame that drives the cover-up; shame that ruins, and sometimes even ends, lives. People willing to honestly examine their own mistakes for others’ benefit deserve some grace in return. The true shame lies with those refusing to offer it.
- 
  Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist
-

In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

title: What the rift within the Tsikhanouski family means for the Belarusian opposition in exile
content_c:
How the Tsikhanouskis' conflict is affecting the Belarusian opposition
October 30, 2026
Blogger and dissident Siarhei Tsikhanouski , 48, was detained in Belarus in May 2020, after he had announced to challenge the country's ruler, Alexander Lukashenko, in the upcoming presidential elections. In December 2021, Tsikhanouski was convicted to 18 years in prison, in part for organizing "mass unrest."
After his arrest his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, took his place and challenged Lukashenko as presidential candidate. Despite allegations of large-scale vote-rigging, Lukashenko was declared the winner of the election in August 2020. This triggered unprecedented mass protests across the country. They were violently suppressed, and thousands of government critics were arrested or fled into exile. Tsikhanouskaya also fled her homeland and became the leading representative of the Belarusian democratic movement.
In June 2025, Siarhei Tsikhanouski was released after nearly five years in prison and was forcibly taken out of the country.
Blogger in exile
Some 14 months after his release, the blogger has re-activated his YouTube channel, where he not only denounces Alexander Lukashenko's regime, but also Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's office, Belarusian media in exile, political analysts and others. Thousands of people follow his streams.
In one of them, Tsikhanouski claims that while Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya obviously enjoyed "a certain legitimacy from the European Union," the people who were living "quietly and silently" in Belarus today had not granted her any. He said that many of those who had voted for her as joint candidate of Belarus' opposition were regretting this today.
What does Tsikhanouski propose?
Tsikhanouski has suggested that a supervisory board should be established under the label "United Office of Demoratic Forces." It would be made up of "former presidential candidates, protest leaders and iconic figures of the revolution," including himself and his wife. "There would not be a full legitimacy but one which was at least granted by Belarusians," Tsikhanouski said, adding that such a supervisory board could oversee the distribution of grant funds.
Speaking about his wife, he said: "Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya was a so-called technical candidate, who received the votes of all those who were against Lukashenko. The percentage of votes she received in the 2020 election was negligible because no one knew who she was. She was allowed to run because she did not pose a threat for the regime, and because she had neither supporters nor political experience."
What's happening in the Tsikhanouski family?
Asked by DW what his goals were, Siarhei Tsikhanouski refused to comment and referred to his livestreams instead. The former political prisoner is residing in the US and is, by his own account, currently unemployed. At the beginning of summer he said he was living in Los Angeles, learning English, preparing for university studies and writing a book. It is also known that his children — a teenage son and a younger daughter — temporarily stayed with him in the US. Today, however, they attend school in Poland, where Tsikhanouskaya resides.
Neither she nor her office have commented on the family situation or her husband's allegations. Even before the public dispute, the leader of the Belarusian democratic forces avoided commenting on her husband. Asked about his activities, she often suggested to approach him directly.
Speaking to DW in December 2025, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya merely said: "What happens in the public sphere and what happens at home, are different things. I understand Siarhei's deep traumatization and also his very strong reactions to certain events. Siarhei was in prison for five years, and I look at it with great understanding. This is why I'm not going public or making any comments. We'll deal with it among ourselves."
Democratic forces in a leadership crisis?
During the 32-year-long rule of the Lukashenko regime, the Belarusian opposition has weathered many crises and conflicts. Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's leadership role has been called into question more than once. However, she and her team have always managed to work themselves out of difficult situations during the last couple of years. But will she still be able to do that now, with her own husband having turned into her critic?
Siarhei Tsikhanouski had gone back to his own self, said political scientist Yury Drakakhrust: "With all his idiosyncrasies, his style of debate, which is not exactly in line with common practice. This is likely to strike many as odd, including Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's international partners."
Tsikhanouski, Drakakhrust pointed out, insisted that he was the key figure of the 2020 events, which is why he was entitled to all the benefits, privileges, recognition and invitations. But there was no way back.
"Even if we assume that Tsikhanouski is right, that he was the central figure, what good would it do today?" he asked. "If, suddenly, hundreds of thousands of Belarusians watched his livestreams, collected funds, formed local groups or associations in Tsikhanouski's name, then perhaps it would be possible to turn back the wheel. But this will hardly be the case."
Drakakhrust described the current situation within the democratic forces as a "crisis." He doubted that Tsikhanouski would be able to reach an agreement with all the members of the supervisory board he has proposed. Furthermore, his wife, in particular, had since established certain assets, resources, and a status for herself through her office.
Tsikhanouskaya — recognized beyond Belarusian borders
"Tsikhanouskaya is being received at high levels, if not as an elected president, then as a leader for Belarus and Belarusian democracy. She's not regarded as just one of several democratic leaders from Belarus," the political scientist said.
He pointed out that not only Tsikhanouskaya, but also other actors from the 2020 election campaign are in exile. They, however, had not achieved a similar level of representation or comparable access to resources. "She has surpassed them as a politician, and that's what counts."
Drakakhrust said that the Belarusian government views disputes among the opposition with a touch of irony, occasionally adding fuel to the fire: "Basically, they don't care who wins. The main thing is that there is conflict, bickering and mutual vilification."
This article was originally published in Russian.

title: Alaska-Wahl: US-Ministerium bestätigt strafrechtliche Ermittlungen im Fall Sullivan gegen Sullivan
content_c:
Sullivan gegen Sullivan US-Ministerium bestätigt strafrechtliche Ermittlungen zu Alaska-Wahl
Das US-Justizministerium hat strafrechtliche Ermittlungen wegen des Versuchs der Wählertäuschung bei der Senatswahl in Alaska bestätigt. »Wenn glaubwürdige Informationen ans Licht kommen, sind wir entschlossen, diesen Hinweisen nachzugehen«, sagte der für Alaska zuständige Bundesanwalt Michael Heyman bei einer Pressekonferenz.
Es gehe um den Verdacht der Täuschung von Wählern. Zu welchen Straftatbeständen genau ermittelt wird, wollte er auch auf Nachfrage nicht erläutern.
Bei dem Fall geht es um zwei Kandidaten, die mit dem nahezu identischen Namen für den US-Senat kandidieren: Amtsinhaber Dan S. Sullivan und der politische Neuling Dan J. Sullivan. Schon länger verdächtigen die Republikaner die Demokraten, mit der Verwechslungsgefahr den Amtsinhaber zu schwächen – auch wenn der Herausforderer Dan J. Sullivan gar nicht für die Demokraten antritt. Beweise lieferten sie bisher nicht.
Wahlzettel mit zwei namensgleichen Kandidaten
Foto: Eloise Brethes / AFP
Die »New York Times« hatte jüngst allerdings berichtet, Verbündete der demokratischen Kandidatin Mary Peltola hätten gezielt nach einem Namensvetter des Amtsinhabers gesucht, um dessen Erfolgschancen zu schmälern. Laut der Zeitung bestreitet Peltolas Wahlkampfteam jegliche Beteiligung an dessen Kandidatur.
Bereits zuvor hatte US-Präsident Donald Trump das Bundesjustizministerium damit beauftragt, Klage gegen den Bundesstaat einzureichen. Damit soll eine Bestätigung der Wahlergebnisse verhindert werden, falls dem republikanischen Amtsinhaber wegen einer Namensverwechslung Stimmen fehlen. An dem Schritt gab es viel Kritik, weil er als Eingriff seitens der US-Regierung in die Wahlen in dem Bundesstaat gewertet wurde.
Bundesanwalt Heyman: Strafrechtliche Ermittlungen wegen des Versuchs der Wählertäuschung
Foto: Justin Sullivan / Getty Images
Der nun von Trump kritisierte Namenstrick ist bei US-Wahlen nicht neu – Demokraten wie Republikaner haben ihn bereits genutzt. 1946 trat ein viermaliger Stadtrat aus Boston namens Joe Russo bei einer demokratischen Vorwahl um einen Sitz im Kongress gegen einen 27-jährigen Hausmeister mit demselben Namen an. Anhänger des dritten Kandidaten im Rennen und späteren Siegers, John F. Kennedy, hatten ihn für die Liste rekrutiert.
In Florida wurde ein demokratischer Staatssenator namens Jose Javier Rodriguez 2020 durch eine Republikanerin und einen weiteren Kandidaten namens Alex Rodriguez herausgefordert. title: Zelda, WoW und GTA VI: Warum die Games noch immer faszinieren
content_c:
Zelda, WoW und GTA VI Warum drei Gaming-Legenden noch immer faszinieren
Zelda, World of Warcraft und Grand Theft Auto: Der November bietet für Gamer gleich drei neu aufgelegte Videospiel-Klassiker. Warum lösen die jahrzehntealten Game-Reihen noch immer solche Begeisterung aus?
Erst das Königreich Hyrule retten, dann mit Freunden durch Azeroth ziehen und zwischendurch noch ein bisschen Chaos in Vice City anrichten: Wer gerne zockt, braucht im November vor allem eines - Zeit. Denn innerhalb von gerade einmal zwei Wochen kehren gleich drei der größten Namen der Gaminggeschichte zurück: Am 5. November erscheinen das Remake von "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" und "World of Warcraft: Forever", am 19. November folgt "Grand Theft Auto VI".
Doch warum lösen drei Spielereihen, die seit Jahrzehnten existieren, noch immer so viel Begeisterung aus?
Drei Spiele, drei Arten von Kult
"The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" gilt fast 30 Jahre nach seiner Veröffentlichung noch immer als eines der besten Videospiele aller Zeiten. Das Fantasyabenteuer von 1998 rund um den Helden Link prägte dreidimensionale Spielwelten und führt mit 99 von 100 Punkten bis heute die Bestenliste der Bewertungsplattform Metacritic an.
"World of Warcraft", kurz WoW, machte ab 2004 das gemeinsame Spielen im Internet zum Massenphänomen. Auf dem Höhepunkt zählte das Online-Rollenspiel mehr als zwölf Millionen Abonnements. WoW konnte ganze Nächte verschlingen und die Fantasywelt Azeroth wurde so für manche zum zweiten Zuhause, mit festen Verabredungen und Freundschaften.
Jason Duval, eine der Hauptfiguren aus der Videospiel-Reihe "Grand Theft Auto"“"
Auch "Grand Theft Auto", kurz GTA, ist längst mehr als eine erfolgreiche Spielereihe. Seine frei erkundbaren Großstädte sind bissige Karikaturen der amerikanischen Gesellschaft, samt Radiosendern mit echten Popsongs und absurden Moderationen. Wegen ihrer Gewaltdarstellungen sorgt die Reihe seit Jahrzehnten für Kontroversen. Auf den nächsten Teil warten Fans inzwischen seit 13 Jahren. Nach mehreren Verschiebungen ist der Release von "GTA VI" selbst zum Internet-Meme geworden: Unwahrscheinliche Dinge, die bereits eingetreten sind, bevor das Spiel erschienen ist.
Warum wir immer wieder zurückkehren
Drei unterschiedliche Erfolgsgeschichten, die eines gemeinsam haben: Ihre Spielwelten sind für Millionen Menschen Teil der eigenen Biografie geworden. Wer nach Jahren durch eine vertraute virtuelle Welt streift, entdeckt dort nicht nur alte Spielorte, sondern auch ein Stück der eigenen Vergangenheit. Manchmal reicht schon eine Melodie, um sich wieder wie damals vor der Konsole zu fühlen.
Dass solche Erinnerungen auch wirtschaftlich etwas wert sind, legt eine Studie von 2025 mit 417 Gamern nahe: Bei bestimmten Spielen können positive Erinnerungen die Kaufbereitschaft für Neuauflagen steigern. Besonders stark kann die nostalgische Bindung bei Spielen aus der eigenen Jugend sein.
Anders als bei Filmen oder Büchern gestalten Menschen in Videospielen ihre Abenteuer selbst mit. Gerade in offenen Spielwelten entscheiden sie, wohin sie gehen und was sie erleben. So bleiben nicht nur Figuren und Geschichten in Erinnerung, sondern werden zu persönlichen Erlebnissen. Und auch zwischen den Veröffentlichungen halten Fans ihre Spielwelten lebendig: Sie tüfteln an eigenen Erweiterungen, diskutieren Details der Spielgeschichte oder machen Szenen zu Internet-Memes.
Die Spieler sind erwachsen geworden
Doch die Gamer, die damals ganze Nächte in Azeroth verbrachten, haben heute womöglich Job, Familie und weniger Freizeit. Laut dem Branchenverband "game" spielen in Deutschland 41,2 Millionen Menschen Videospiele, im Durchschnitt sind sie 38,3 Jahre alt. Die Jugendlichen, die in den 2000er-Jahren zockten, sind längst erwachsen geworden – und spielen heute noch.
Damit haben sich die Ansprüche an das Hobby verändert: Was früher ganze Nächte füllen durfte, muss heute in einen Feierabend passen. Und die Spiele haben sich entsprechend angepasst. Bei World of Warcraft wurden viele Abläufe über die Jahre schneller und bequemer. Für manche Herausforderungen braucht man heute keine feste Gruppe mehr, Mitspieler werden automatisch zusammengeführt. Damit wurde die Zusammenarbeit in manchen Bereichen des Spiels nicht mehr notwendig.
Mit "World of Warcraft: Forever" will Entwickler Blizzard nun aber wieder stärker auf gemeinsame Abenteuer setzen. Die neue Version greift die ursprüngliche Spielwelt auf und erweitert sie um neue Inhalte. Ob sich damit auch das frühere Gemeinschaftsgefühl zurückholen lässt, bleibt offen.
Das Videospiel “World of Warcraft: Forever" erweitert die ursprüngliche Spielwelt um neue Inhalte.
Nostalgie als Milliardengeschäft
Was für Fans eine Rückkehr in die eigene Vergangenheit ist, ist für die Gamesindustrie dabei ein Geschäft mit vertrauten Marken. Allein in Deutschland wurden 2025 mit Videospielen, Hardware und Online-Diensten rund 9,4 Milliarden Euro umgesetzt. Große Spieleproduktionen verschlingen teils Hunderte Millionen Dollar. Bekannte Namen bringen ein vorhandenes Publikum und Aufmerksamkeit mit, lange bevor ein neues Spiel erscheint.
Dass bekannte Marken nicht zwangsläufig für Stillstand stehen, zeigt ausgerechnet der Klassiker "Zelda". Mit "Breath of the Wild" veränderte Nintendo 2017 die Spielprinzipien der Reihe so grundlegend, dass die Reihe auch Menschen begeisterte, die nicht mit den Spielen der Neunzigerjahre aufgewachsen sind - mehr als 34 Millionen Exemplare wurden verkauft.
Die drei November-Veröffentlichungen zeigen dabei nun unterschiedliche Strategien: Nintendo legt mit "Ocarina of Time" einen Klassiker neu auf. Blizzard greift wiederum mit "Forever" frühere Spielprinzipien wieder auf. Und Rockstar entwickelt mit GTA VI eine eigenständige Fortsetzung. Deren Vorgänger GTA V kam nach Herstellerangaben auf mehr als 230 Millionen ausgelieferte und digital verkaufte Exemplare.
Alte Spiele, neues Leben
Trotzdem stellt sich die Frage, wie viel Platz für neue Ideen bleibt, wenn die großen Namen so viel Aufmerksamkeit bekommen. Unabhängige Studios setzen mit ungewöhnlichen Konzepten immer wieder neue Impulse. Die etablierten Reihen müssen dagegen alte Fans halten und gleichzeitig eine neue Generation gewinnen.
Hyrule retten, Azeroth erkunden, Vice City unsicher machen: Die Möglichkeiten im November sind gewaltig, die Freizeit vieler Fans dürfte hingegen begrenzt sein. Vielleicht ist das die größte Herausforderung für die Rückkehr der drei Legenden: Können sie noch einmal dieselbe Begeisterung auslösen, wenn sich der Alltag der Menschen vor den Bildschirmen längst verändert hat? An der Vorfreude ihrer Fans dürfte es jedenfalls nicht scheitern.

title: Serbien nach Aleksandar Vucics Wahlniederlage: Die siegereichen Anhänger der Studierenden-Liste werden ungeduldig
content_c:
Serbien nach Vucic: Die Sieger werden ungeduldig
30. Oktober 2026
Aleksandar Vucic ist großes Kino gewohnt. Jahrelang begleiteten ihm ergebene Medien jeden Schritt des einst allmächtigen Präsidenten Serbiens. Seine TikTok-Auftritte eröffneten die Abendnachrichten. Dann verlor er am 25.10.2026 die Wahl gegen die Studierendenliste. Seitdem ist vieles anders.
Die Sieger übten "revolutionären Terror" aus, klagte Vucic auf einer Pressekonferenz vor weniger Mikrofonen als früher. "Wenn sie den Terror gegen Andersdenkende fortsetzen - die Prügelattacken, die Verwüstungen und alles andere -, während die staatlichen Stellen nichts unternehmen, werden wir gezwungen sein, uns selbst zu organisieren", drohte er.
Als "Terror" gilt ihm etwa der sofortige Rücktritt der Direktorin des öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunks RTS. Auch führende Redakteure wurden abgelöst.
Am Montag (26.10.2026) drang eine kleine Gruppe in den TV-Sender Informer ein, gegen den wegen der Dämonisierung von Vucic-Kritikern in den vergangenen Jahren Tausende Klagen eingereicht worden waren. Journalistenverbände beantragen nun den Lizenzentzug.
Andere Vucic-treue Boulevardmedien haben bereits den Ton geändert: Anders als Informer nennen sie die Studierendenliste nicht mehr "Terroristen" und "Söldner".
Alte Vorwürfe gegen Vucic
Seit die von der Studentenrevolte getragene Liste aus Professoren, Aktivisten und Künstlern am 25. Oktober 53 Prozent holte, überschlagen sich die Ereignisse. Vucics Serbische Fortschrittspartei (SNS) blieb bei 39 Prozent.
In vielen Orten trugen Bürger friedlich Vucic-Porträts aus den Rathäusern. Die Staatsanwaltschaft für organisierte Kriminalität ermittelt unter anderem wegen Wahlmanipulationen. Eine Sonderkommission prüft die Höhere Staatsanwaltschaft Belgrad, die laut Kritikern Vucic diente und seine Gegner verfolgte.
Die Vorwürfe gegen ihn sind alt: Er und sein System hätten Medien an der kurzen Leine gehalten, nur loyale Firmen hätten Staatsaufträge erhalten, Vucic, seine Partei und der serbische Staat hätten Verbindungen zur organisierten Kriminalität.
Auslöser der Revolte war vor zwei Jahren der Einsturz des frisch renovierten Bahnhofsvordachs in Novi Sad. 16 Menschen starben. Das Unglück konnte sich vermutlich ereignen, weil bei der Auftragsvergabe zur Renovierung des Bahnhofs Korruption und Pfusch eine Rolle gespielt hatten.
Jetzt wächst die Ungeduld jener Bürger, die eben noch auf den Straßen feierten. Das neue Parlament muss erst zusammentreten, viele Machthebel hält noch die SNS in der Hand. "Eine Gesellschaft, die so lange von einer Partei unterdrückt wurde, die sich wie ein Feudalherr verhielt, erwartet jetzt verständlicherweise Gerechtigkeit", sagt Dejan Bursac vom Belgrader Institut für Philosophie und Gesellschaftstheorie der DW. "In diesem Machtvakuum sind die Bürger ungeduldig."
Vucic und führende Funktionäre versprechen eine starke Opposition und baldige Rückkehr, sobald "die da" das Land ruiniert hätten. Die meisten Kritiker verlangen dagegen Ermittlungen und Anklagen gegen Vucic. "Die Leute von der SNS benehmen sich, als hätten sie irgendwo im demokratischen Skandinavien die Bezirkswahl verloren - und nicht, als seien sie Teil eines zutiefst korrupten und kriminellen Regimes", sagt Bursac.
Wie sehr kann die alte Regierung der neuen schaden?
In Serbien sind politische Seitenwechsler verbreitet: Man geht dorthin, wo die Macht sitzt. Auch Vucic räumt ein, dass viele bisherige Mitstreiter ihm nun den Rücken kehren. "Wir werden Fälle erleben, in denen sie zurücktreten oder sich bedeckt halten, sich sogar als Informanten für die künftige Regierung anbieten", sagt Zlatko Minic von "Transparenz Serbien", einer Organisation, die Regierungen beobachtet. Die Frage, bei der es buchstäblich um viele Millionen Dollar gehe, laute: Wie sehr könne die alte Regierung der neuen schaden? "Viele Amtsträger haben noch Zeit, Aufträge zu vergeben und die von ihnen geführten Behörden finanziell zu verpflichten, ohne sich dabei womöglich selbst strafbar zu machen", warnt Minic.
Allerdings hat die Studierendenliste laut Kennern längst Kontakte zu Gegnern von Vucics Regierungsstil in Polizei und Verwaltung. Die Wahlsieger könnten nun bestimmte Machenschaften verhindern. Am Mittwoch (28.10.2026) forderte die Liste erneut Rücktritte an der Spitze von Polizei und Justiz. Hinweisgeber sollten sich melden, falls die scheidende Regierung "Unterlagen vernichten" sollte.
Ihre erste Pressekonferenz hielten Vertreter der Studierendenliste symbolisch im Pionierpark vor dem Parlament ab. Den hatten Vucics Anhänger Anfang 2025 eingezäunt und zum Pro-Regierungs-Zeltcamp gemacht. Laut investigativen Journalisten versammelten sich dort auch Schläger und Kriminelle, die Demonstranten angriffen. Am Morgen nach dem Wahlsieg räumten Unterstützer der Studierendenliste den Park auf.
Kein außenpolitischer Kurswechsel
Die siegreiche Studierendenliste vereint Linke und Rechte, proeuropäische und prorussische Kräfte. Im Mittelpunkt stehen innenpolitische Veränderungen. Die EU-Beitrittsgespräche will die Liste mit echten Reformen vorantreiben. Sanktionen gegen Russland und eine Anerkennung Kosovos lehnt sie ab - womit auch die Bevölkerung in Serbien nahezu einhellig übereinstimmt.
"Unser Plan ist, das Land zu stabilisieren und zu entwickeln, nicht, es durch irgendeine abrupte außenpolitische Kursänderung zu destabilisieren", sagt der Psychologieprofessor und künftige Abgeordnete Oliver Toskovic der DW.
Die EU werde anders als unter Vucic nicht als "Deckmantel" missbraucht. Der Beitrittsprozess Serbiens stockte zuletzt, während Vucic dem "Westen" vorwarf, eine "Farbrevolution in Serbien" angezettelt zu haben.
"Bei der Energie sind wir stark von Russland abhängig. Das ist zwar ein Fehler der bisherigen Regierung", sagt Toskovic. "Aber deshalb würden Sanktionen den Staat derzeit destabilisieren. Und das wäre weder für uns noch für die EU gut." Wie sich allerdings die Energiepolitik unter einer Regierung der Studierendenliste entwickeln wird, ist noch unklar.
Wo Vucic Giftpfeile Richtung Kosovo, Kroatien oder Bosnien und Herzegowina schoss, versprechen führende Vertreter der neuen Liste Entspannung und bessere Beziehungen. So erklärte Ilija Srdanovic, Spitzenkandidat der Studierendenliste, zum Verhältnis zu Kosovo, man sei zum Dialog mit der Regierung in der kosovarischen Hauptstadt Prishtina bereit. Mit dem kroatischen Ministerpräsidenten hat er bereits telefoniert.
Noch ist die Wahl allerdings nicht abgeschlossen: Am Sonntag, dem 1. November, wird wegen Unregelmäßigkeiten in rund fünfzig Wahllokalen erneut abgestimmt. Danach kann das Parlament zusammentreten. Eine schnelle Regierungsbildung wäre keine Überraschung. Die Namen der Mitglieder bleiben vorerst geheim.

Serbien nach Vucic: Die Sieger werden ungeduldig
30. Oktober 2026
Aleksandar Vucic ist großes Kino gewohnt. Jahrelang begleiteten ihm ergebene Medien jeden Schritt des einst allmächtigen Präsidenten Serbiens. Seine TikTok-Auftritte eröffneten die Abendnachrichten. Dann verlor er am 25.10.2026 die Wahl gegen die Studierendenliste. Seitdem ist vieles anders.
Die Sieger übten "revolutionären Terror" aus, klagte Vucic auf einer Pressekonferenz vor weniger Mikrofonen als früher. "Wenn sie den Terror gegen Andersdenkende fortsetzen - die Prügelattacken, die Verwüstungen und alles andere -, während die staatlichen Stellen nichts unternehmen, werden wir gezwungen sein, uns selbst zu organisieren", drohte er.
Als "Terror" gilt ihm etwa der sofortige Rücktritt der Direktorin des öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunks RTS. Auch führende Redakteure wurden abgelöst.
Am Montag (26.10.2026) drang eine kleine Gruppe in den TV-Sender Informer ein, gegen den wegen der Dämonisierung von Vucic-Kritikern in den vergangenen Jahren Tausende Klagen eingereicht worden waren. Journalistenverbände beantragen nun den Lizenzentzug.
Andere Vucic-treue Boulevardmedien haben bereits den Ton geändert: Anders als Informer nennen sie die Studierendenliste nicht mehr "Terroristen" und "Söldner".
Alte Vorwürfe gegen Vucic
Seit die von der Studentenrevolte getragene Liste aus Professoren, Aktivisten und Künstlern am 25. Oktober 53 Prozent holte, überschlagen sich die Ereignisse. Vucics Serbische Fortschrittspartei (SNS) blieb bei 39 Prozent.
In vielen Orten trugen Bürger friedlich Vucic-Porträts aus den Rathäusern. Die Staatsanwaltschaft für organisierte Kriminalität ermittelt unter anderem wegen Wahlmanipulationen. Eine Sonderkommission prüft die Höhere Staatsanwaltschaft Belgrad, die laut Kritikern Vucic diente und seine Gegner verfolgte.
Die Vorwürfe gegen ihn sind alt: Er und sein System hätten Medien an der kurzen Leine gehalten, nur loyale Firmen hätten Staatsaufträge erhalten, Vucic, seine Partei und der serbische Staat hätten Verbindungen zur organisierten Kriminalität.
Auslöser der Revolte war vor zwei Jahren der Einsturz des frisch renovierten Bahnhofsvordachs in Novi Sad. 16 Menschen starben. Das Unglück konnte sich vermutlich ereignen, weil bei der Auftragsvergabe zur Renovierung des Bahnhofs Korruption und Pfusch eine Rolle gespielt hatten.
Jetzt wächst die Ungeduld jener Bürger, die eben noch auf den Straßen feierten. Das neue Parlament muss erst zusammentreten, viele Machthebel hält noch die SNS in der Hand. "Eine Gesellschaft, die so lange von einer Partei unterdrückt wurde, die sich wie ein Feudalherr verhielt, erwartet jetzt verständlicherweise Gerechtigkeit", sagt Dejan Bursac vom Belgrader Institut für Philosophie und Gesellschaftstheorie der DW. "In diesem Machtvakuum sind die Bürger ungeduldig."
Vucic und führende Funktionäre versprechen eine starke Opposition und baldige Rückkehr, sobald "die da" das Land ruiniert hätten. Die meisten Kritiker verlangen dagegen Ermittlungen und Anklagen gegen Vucic. "Die Leute von der SNS benehmen sich, als hätten sie irgendwo im demokratischen Skandinavien die Bezirkswahl verloren - und nicht, als seien sie Teil eines zutiefst korrupten und kriminellen Regimes", sagt Bursac.
Wie sehr kann die alte Regierung der neuen schaden?
In Serbien sind politische Seitenwechsler verbreitet: Man geht dorthin, wo die Macht sitzt. Auch Vucic räumt ein, dass viele bisherige Mitstreiter ihm nun den Rücken kehren. "Wir werden Fälle erleben, in denen sie zurücktreten oder sich bedeckt halten, sich sogar als Informanten für die künftige Regierung anbieten", sagt Zlatko Minic von "Transparenz Serbien", einer Organisation, die Regierungen beobachtet. Die Frage, bei der es buchstäblich um viele Millionen Dollar gehe, laute: Wie sehr könne die alte Regierung der neuen schaden? "Viele Amtsträger haben noch Zeit, Aufträge zu vergeben und die von ihnen geführten Behörden finanziell zu verpflichten, ohne sich dabei womöglich selbst strafbar zu machen", warnt Minic.
Allerdings hat die Studierendenliste laut Kennern längst Kontakte zu Gegnern von Vucics Regierungsstil in Polizei und Verwaltung. Die Wahlsieger könnten nun bestimmte Machenschaften verhindern. Am Mittwoch (28.10.2026) forderte die Liste erneut Rücktritte an der Spitze von Polizei und Justiz. Hinweisgeber sollten sich melden, falls die scheidende Regierung "Unterlagen vernichten" sollte.
Ihre erste Pressekonferenz hielten Vertreter der Studierendenliste symbolisch im Pionierpark vor dem Parlament ab. Den hatten Vucics Anhänger Anfang 2025 eingezäunt und zum Pro-Regierungs-Zeltcamp gemacht. Laut investigativen Journalisten versammelten sich dort auch Schläger und Kriminelle, die Demonstranten angriffen. Am Morgen nach dem Wahlsieg räumten Unterstützer der Studierendenliste den Park auf.
Kein außenpolitischer Kurswechsel
Die siegreiche Studierendenliste vereint Linke und Rechte, proeuropäische und prorussische Kräfte. Im Mittelpunkt stehen innenpolitische Veränderungen. Die EU-Beitrittsgespräche will die Liste mit echten Reformen vorantreiben. Sanktionen gegen Russland und eine Anerkennung Kosovos lehnt sie ab - womit auch die Bevölkerung in Serbien nahezu einhellig übereinstimmt.
"Unser Plan ist, das Land zu stabilisieren und zu entwickeln, nicht, es durch irgendeine abrupte außenpolitische Kursänderung zu destabilisieren", sagt der Psychologieprofessor und künftige Abgeordnete Oliver Toskovic der DW.
Die EU werde anders als unter Vucic nicht als "Deckmantel" missbraucht. Der Beitrittsprozess Serbiens stockte zuletzt, während Vucic dem "Westen" vorwarf, eine "Farbrevolution in Serbien" angezettelt zu haben.
"Bei der Energie sind wir stark von Russland abhängig. Das ist zwar ein Fehler der bisherigen Regierung", sagt Toskovic. "Aber deshalb würden Sanktionen den Staat derzeit destabilisieren. title: Польша подтвердила передачу Украине истребителей МиГ-29
content_c:
Министр обороны Польши Владислав Косиняк-Камыш объявил о передаче Украине двух истребителей МиГ-29. Об этом он сообщил 30 октября во время визита на 12-ю базу беспилотной авиации в Мирославце.
По его словам, польская армия постепенно выводит эти самолеты из эксплуатации. Взамен польская сторона рассчитывает получить от Украины беспилотные летательные аппараты.
"Польша готовит очередной пакет помощи Украине. Масштабы поддержки ограничены соображениями безопасности польского государства и ресурсами вооруженных сил, как это определено начальником Генерального штаба. Как заявил министр национальной обороны, мы готовим поддержку для техники, которая выводится из эксплуатации польскими вооруженными силами (срок ее службы подходит к концу), техники, которая не используется польской армией, но могла бы пригодиться в Украине», — сообщило Министерство национальной обороны.
По данным газеты Rzeczpospolita, один из истребителей до сих пор пригоден к полётам, тогда как срок эксплуатации второго уже истек. Помимо боевых самолетов, Польша предоставит Украине, в частности, комплект артиллерийских боеприпасов калибра 155 мм и 152 мм, 20-калиберные 102-мм снаряды для шестиствольных пушек истребителей F-16, которые используются, в частности, для сбивания российских беспилотников.
В сентябре Министерство обороны Украины сообщало о новом пакете военной помощи от Польши стоимостью около 50 млн евро.
Напомним, что в 2022 и 2023 годах Польша незаметно отправила в Украину 14 МиГ-29, которые находились в различном состоянии. Задачи списанных МиГ-29 выполняют F-16 и первые 12 корейских FA-50, которые достигнут полной оперативной готовности в 2026 году. Вице-премьер и министр национальной обороны Владислав Косиняк-Камыш (ПСЛ) тогда заявил, что передача техники Украине будет выгодна польской армии, поскольку она получит взамен технологии беспилотных летательных аппаратов и ракет.

title: Польська євродепутатка Зайончковська-Гернік оприлюднила сатиричне "розпорядження" про відсторонення прем'єра Туска на тлі кризи в Конституційному трибуналі
content_c:
Депутатка Європейського парламенту від польської правої коаліції "Конфедерація" Ева Зайончковська-Гернік опублікувала сатиричне "розпорядження" про нібито негайне призупинення повноважень прем'єр-міністра Польщі Дональда Туска у відповідь на дії судді Анни Корвін-Пйотровської в Конституційному трибуналі (КТ).
"Я оголошую негайну перерву в діяльності прем'єр-міністра Дональда Туска, включно з виконанням нагляду за всіма правоохоронними службами та спеціальними службами. Сподіваюся, що цей документ буде сприйнятий з такою ж серйозністю, як той папірець пані Корвін-Пйотровської, яка таким самим чином замінила голову КТ під диктат банди Туска", – написала євродепутатка в соціальній мережі X.
В оприлюдненому документі, датованому 30 жовтня 2026 року, політикиня іронічно вказала, що діє як особа, яка "має найдовший стаж серед депутатів Європарламенту 1990 року народження та вміє посилатися на правові підстави, що не мають адекватного застосування, так само як пані Анна Корвін-Пйотровська".
Підставами для свого символічного рішення Зайончковська-Гернік назвала залучення силових відомств до вирішення політичних суперечок, координацію дій прокуратури, поліції та політиків "Громадянської коаліції" для усунення неугодних уряду суддів КТ, а також "силове захоплення Конституційного трибуналу виконавчою владою в час, коли поляки зазвичай зосереджуються на вшануванні пам'яті своїх померлих близьких" (напередодні Дня всіх святих – ІФ-У).
Як повідомлялося, у п'ятницю ввечері перед будівлею Конституційного трибуналу на алеї Шуха у Варшаві спалахнули протести за участю лідерів опозиційних партій "Право і справедливість" (PiS) та "Конфедерація", під час яких учасники акції за вказівкою голови трибуналу Богдана Свєнчковського перерізали ланцюг на воротах огорожі. Водночас у столичній поліції заявили, що охороняють зовнішній периметр установи на підставі офіційних звернень Генерального прокурора та одного із суддів КТ через загрозу громадському порядку, а також повідомили про затримання трьох осіб, які перелізли через паркан.

Підставами для свого символічного рішення Зайончковська-Гернік назвала залучення силових відомств до вирішення політичних суперечок, координацію дій прокуратури, поліції та політиків "Громадянської коаліції" для усунення неугодних уряду суддів КТ, а також "силове захоплення Конституційного трибуналу виконавчою владою в час, коли поляки зазвичай зосереджуються на вшануванні пам'яті своїх померлих близьких" (напередодні Дня всіх святих – ІФ-У).
Як повідомлялося, у п'ятницю ввечері перед будівлею Конституційного трибуналу на алеї Шуха у Варшаві спалахнули протести за участю лідерів опозиційних партій "Право і справедливість" (PiS) та "Конфедерація", під час яких учасники акції за вказівкою голови трибуналу Богдана Свєнчковського перерізали ланцюг на воротах огорожі. Водночас у столичній поліції заявили, що охороняють зовнішній периметр установи на підставі офіційних звернень Генерального прокурора та одного із суддів КТ через загрозу громадському порядку, а також повідомили про затримання трьох осіб, які перелізли через паркан.

title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
content_c:
US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
- Published
US death row inmate Christa Pike has released her first public statement since her botched execution in September.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said in the statement.
"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Pike, 50, was discharged from hospital at the end of last month after surviving two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital, which left her in a critical condition.
She has since been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
Pike is thought to be the only person to survive an execution attempt by lethal injection.
- I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's 
  - Published2 October
- What happened in Christa Pike's failed US execution, and how did she survive? 
  - Published14 hours ago
"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," she said in her statement on Friday. "But healing is not the same as being okay."
Her lawyers previously said she had suffered from pneumonia following the attempted execution, had significant swelling on her arms and was also unable to swallow.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike's botched execution captivated and shocked the world last month and shocked Pike, too.
"I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I'm deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position," she said in her statement.
Bethany Mann, a friend of Pike's and a founder of Child Arise Tennessee, which supports children and families affected by parental incarceration, told the BBC on Friday that she had been in direct contact with Pike since the botched execution attempt.
When asked about her reaction to Pike's statement, Mann said: "Truthfully, I don't know that I have anything to add to what Christa has already expressed so powerfully herself, and I want to be respectful of her privacy."
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee paused all executions for the remainder of the year and ordered an independent review to "determine exactly what occurred".
Lee was asked by reporters this week about a potential second execution attempt. "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts," he responded.
Speaking about the state's response to what happened to Pike, Mann said: "I find it deeply troubling that, even after what Christa endured, Governor Lee has shown little public willingness to reconsider the death penalty itself, rather than simply the procedures used to carry it out."
She added: "What happened to Christa is not an isolated tragedy, nor should this conversation begin and end with her."
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not explained why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.
It declined comment on Pike's statement when contacted by the BBC.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death and attended the botched execution, later calling it a "mess".
She told a local ABC News affiliate in Florida, where she lives, that she thinks the state owes her an apology.
"All I wanted was justice," Martinez said.
Pike was the first woman scheduled to be executed in the state of Tennessee in over 200 years.
Her lawyers have spent decades appealing her case. In the days leading up to her scheduled execution, both the US Supreme Court and Lee declined to block the execution.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.
  - Published8 October

title: First minister says Welsh spending powers takes step forward after Andy Burnham meeting
content_c:
First minister says Welsh spending powers takes step forward after Andy Burnham meeting
- Published
Welsh First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth says there has been a "significant step forward" with regards to his country's spending and borrowing powers after meeting the prime minister.
Andy Burnham held a meeting of his National Economic Council with the first ministers of Wales and Scotland on Friday, after which ap Iorwerth said it was a matter of "how and when" a loosening of financial restrictions will take place.
At the summit in Glasgow, Burnham lobbied the government leaders to devolve "deeper" to the regions of Wales and Scotland.
The prime minister said the two first ministers had agreed to work with him on "regional empowerment".
No timescales were announced for changes to Wales' finances.
Friday's meeting followed rows between the Welsh and UK government over the chancellor's Budget on Wednesday, which ap Iorwerth had said was "not serious about Wales".
His party Plaid Cymru said the budget left the Welsh government with a real-terms cut in funding, which the UK government denied.
Ap Iorwerth had set out a range of demands to the prime minister in a letter sent at the start of October.
As well as calling for powers over policing and justice, and for more funding for rail projects, he called for an end to restrictions on access to the Wales reserve - spare funding that the Welsh government can store in one year to use in another.
It is capped at £385m, and the Welsh government can only draw down £137.5m and £55m for resource and capital spend respectively per year.
The Welsh government can also borrow up to £1.1bn for infrastructure, with a limit of £165m a year.
Ap Iorwerth said: "There were some real positives here.
"On fiscal flexibility, the ability for us to use our funding better in Wales, use our reserves better in Wales - and on borrowing powers, I was told clearly that its now was a matter of how and when. That is a significant step forward."
He said there was "clearly an interest" for the prime minister to "really understand that sheer injustice of underfunding of rail in Wales that we have seen for many years".
"That is a particular issue we will be taking forward now between my office and his," he said.
On policing, the first minister said "I think instinctively the prime minister wants to go there and there's still work to do".
At a speech this month the first minister called for "practical agreement" on how the two governments could work together on the economy, calling for Westminster to avoid duplication in areas that are devolved already to the Welsh government.
Burnham said Friday's meeting was "positive", and that both first ministers had agreed to "work together jointly on regional empowerment in Scotland and Wales as well".
"We now have a process where we have detailed work by officials on both sides to see if we can come to a set of arrangements that are right for Scotland and right for Wales," Burnham said.
"We had a good discussion today on two fronts, one around re-industrialisation and the offer of more devolution of innovation funding to the regional level."
He said it was for Scotland and Wales to decide how that looks.
Burnham also said the UK government will now look at arrangements for further devolution of employment support.
Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock fiscal flexibilities and borrowing was on the agenda for future Welsh government discussions with No 10 North.
"It is going to take some conversations on how that would work in practice.
"I can't give you a specific time frame as things stand," he said.
Following Wednesday's Budget, which saw an extra £450m announced for Wales over the next three years as well as funding for individual projects, the Welsh government claimed the extra money would represent a real-terms cut to its own finances.
A £30m funding pledge for a new railway station in Cardiff was also described as "an insult" by Wales' transport minister.
On Radio Wales Breakfast on Friday before the summit, ap Iorwerth said there were "paltry sums of money coming on rail, when they've said there's £14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services".
"The Budget was not serious about Wales," he said.
He said in another interview he could "only assume that the prime minister is holding something back".
After the meeting, Downing Street said ap Iorwerth had "agreed to start a process to explore how each government could contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode".
"This would be a policy sprint led by No 10 North, involving officials from each government, to take this agenda forward," they said.
Ap Iorwerth said in a statement: "There was an encouraging consensus that the fiscal and borrowing powers which have for so long put Wales at a disadvantage compared with other UK nations must be revised as a matter of urgency.
"I welcome the prime minister's comments that this is now a matter of how and when."
Welsh ministers had called for changes to their borrowing rules and assurances that child poverty payments it wants to introduce would leave recipients' tax and benefits allowances unaffected.
None of that was addressed in the Budget, although Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock has said "positive" talks were continuing regarding the child poverty payments.
Friday's meeting of the National Economic Council - a summit to help boost the UK economy - was due to be attended by the prime minister and all the devolved leaders.
However, it emerged on Thursday that Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill would not be there after her attendance was blocked by her Democratic Unionist Party (DUP).
Since he became prime minister, Burnham has consistently spoken in favour of devolution.
He has said he is "open" to transferring powers over policing and justice to Wales and, during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, he said he was "ready to make an offer" on the devolution of employment support.

title: Riot police deployed to Poland’s constitutional court after judge suspended
content_c:
Riot police were locked in a tense standoff with protesters outside Poland’s constitutional court on Friday night after its top judge was suspended in the latest escalation in a decade-long dispute over the court’s legal status.
The clashes followed a controversial decision by a group of government-appointed judges to suspend the court’s contested president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, amid disagreements over the bench’s legitimacy.
The move prompted a furious reaction from the rightwing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, with its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, condemning what he claimed was an “assault” on the court.
The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over EU law and the European Union accused Poland’s highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time.
The PiS-backed conservative president, Karol Nawrocki, a close ally of Donald Trump, turned his plane around en route to a state visit in Senegal to return to Warsaw and intervene at the court on Friday night.
Hundreds of protesters – including opposition MPs – gathered outside the building to show their support for the suspended judges. Three people were reportedly arrested for trying to force entry through a heavy police presence.
Shortly before 1am on Saturday, Nawrocki appeared outside the court and made his way through the police cordon, with one video showing the president tussling with security and other judges to force his entry into the building. As of 4am local time, the president remained inside the building.
In a clip posted online, Nawrocki was heard saying the government appointees “were not judges of the constitutional court”.
In a statement read out on his behalf outside the court at 5am, Nawrocki criticised “a violation of Poland’s constitutional order”, saying “a constitutional body was seized by force”. He called for security forces to leave the premises.
The latest clash is likely to further polarise the country, setting the scene for a dramatic showdown in next year’s parliamentary election, with polls showing the populist-right with a chance to return to power.
The court has been at the centre of a dispute dating back to 2015, when the outgoing centrist and the incoming rightwing governments moved in quick succession with legally questionable moves to stack the bench with their appointees.
The dispute over the appointments paralysed the court, followed by further attempts to cripple it during the PiS’s eight years of illiberal rule marred by clashes with the EU over the rule of law.
Since returning to power in 2023, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has repeatedly pledged to reverse controversial reforms as he sought to mend relations with Brussels, while refusing to recognise the court’s legitimacy in the current form.
However, his efforts have been thwarted by opposition-aligned presidents who used their veto powers and expansive interpretations of their powers to block reforms.
In the latest twist this year, Nawrocki, who unexpectedly won last year’s presidential election against Tusk’s candidate, refused to swear in five judges elected by the current parliament, further complicating the legal situation.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe’s advisory body on the rule of law, the Venice Commission, said the president’s refusal should not prevent judges from taking up their posts.
On Friday night, a group of judges elected by the current majority moved to suspend Święczkowski, a former minister under PiS, and seize procedural control of the court. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – who is one of the five judges not accepted by Nawrocki – said she had assumed the top position, citing the longest experience in the judiciary.
Experts are deeply divided in their opinion on the legality of the judge’s suspension. Marcin Matczak, a prominent law expert and outspoken critic of PiS, said he “did not think he would ever end up defending” Święczkowski, but believed the legal basis for his suspension was “non-existent”.
Separately, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said he had asked for Święczkowski and deputy chief Sochański to be stripped of their legal immunity to face prosecution for obstructing the court’s work.
Despite criticism, Tusk insisted that “restoring the rule of law is our duty.”
“After years of PiS’s lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he argued.
Earlier this month, he pledged “the court will begin its work in accordance with the constitution, whether people like it or not.”
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski told reporters on the margins of a G20 meeting in Atlanta that “the constitutional tribunal was politicised under the previous government.”
“What is happening has the purpose of allowing the majority of duly elected judges to make the tribunal function again,” he said.
Opposition leaders and the court’s social media account accused the government of carrying out a judicial “a coup d’état”. Several European far-right figures, including Britain’s Nigel Farage, Liz Truss and the Netherlands’ Geert Wilders, also condemned the move.
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said in a post on X: “The events unfolding tonight … are very serious.”
“Both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why,” he said. “Whatever the facts ultimately establish, thousands gathering outside the tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse.”

Earlier this month, the Council of Europe’s advisory body on the rule of law, the Venice Commission, said the president’s refusal should not prevent judges from taking up their posts.
On Friday night, a group of judges elected by the current majority moved to suspend Święczkowski, a former minister under PiS, and seize procedural control of the court. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – who is one of the five judges not accepted by Nawrocki – said she had assumed the top position, citing the longest experience in the judiciary.
Experts are deeply divided in their opinion on the legality of the judge’s suspension. Marcin Matczak, a prominent law expert and outspoken critic of PiS, said he “did not think he would ever end up defending” Święczkowski, but believed the legal basis for his suspension was “non-existent”.
Separately, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said he had asked for Święczkowski and deputy chief Sochański to be stripped of their legal immunity to face prosecution for obstructing the court’s work.
Despite criticism, Tusk insisted that “restoring the rule of law is our duty.”
“After years of PiS’s lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he argued.
Earlier this month, he pledged “the court will begin its work in accordance with the constitution, whether people like it or not.”
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski told reporters on the margins of a G20 meeting in Atlanta that “the constitutional tribunal was politicised under the previous government.”
“What is happening has the purpose of allowing the majority of duly elected judges to make the tribunal function again,” he said.
Opposition leaders and the court’s social media account accused the government of carrying out a judicial “a coup d’état”. Several European far-right figures, including Britain’s Nigel Farage, Liz Truss and the Netherlands’ Geert Wilders, also condemned the move.
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said in a post on X: “The events unfolding tonight … are very serious.”
“Both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why,” he said. “Whatever the facts ultimately establish, thousands gathering outside the tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse.”

title: Digested week: The Traitors suddenly feels tired – time for a politicians version? | John Crace
content_c:
Monday
You would have thought someone would have made an intervention by now. To save Liz Truss from the worst excesses and delusions of herself. Most former prime ministers – and there are enough of them by now – make the transition into civilian life with little fuss. More or less. John Major found himself elevated from national joke to statesman after 20 years; Tony Blair took the grandiose step of establishing his very own institute; Boris Johnson took his grumblings to the Daily Mail where he is now more or less ignored; Theresa May opted for obscurity; we have yet to find out Keir Starmer’s next move. Yet Liz Truss seems permanently scarred by her 49 days in office and its abrupt ending. Constantly feeling the need to pick away at the wound that will never heal.
She has been abandoned by a Tory party for whom she is nothing but an embarrassment and now finds herself posting conversations on YouTube with people as deranged as herself for just a handful of viewers. And now she has written a 95-page book that is essentially a distillation of her previous book. Just even worse and a bit more desperate. Having read the book for a Digested Read, I would suggest you give it a miss. It reads as one extended cry for help. Still insisting that her budget was derailed by the Bank selling gilts the day before – something she had personally signed off – and that the establishment had been out to get her. She is like a broken record. Time for her family and friends to step in.
Tuesday
There are some footballers who will be for ever Tottenham. At least for me. There was Jimmy Greaves. He may have played for Chelsea, AC Milan and West Ham too but it is White Hart Lane for which he is most remembered. Likewise Gareth Bale. He won all sorts with Real Madrid but for Spurs fans he will always be one of us. Even if, in retirement, he seems at his happiest when he is playing golf. Then there is Harry Kane. Arguably the greatest of the three. The footballer who seemed to have less raw talent than Greaves and Bale but forged himself into the world’s best striker by sheer will and hard work.
I was lucky to see almost all of the home games – and many of the away ones – during Kane’s 11-year stay at the club. It would be nice to be able to say I spotted his ability from the off. But I didn’t. I assumed that, like many academy players who were being sent out on loan, he would eventually be shipped out to a lower league club. But when he did get his first-team chance, he scored goals. And kept on scoring them for a decade. A proper team player. As happy making goals for the team as he was knocking them in. Well, almost. A striker measures their seasons in goals. And he acknowledged the fans. When the team had played badly and lost, most of the rest of the players couldn’t wait to leave the pitch. Harry always made sure to thank the fans for their support.
Nor was I that sad when he joined Bayern Munich. I thought he had earned the move. He had given us more than enough and deserved the chance to play for a club that regularly won something. This week he won the Ballon d’Or and I couldn’t have been happier. Some may have thought it a reward for all the goals he scored for Bayern and England in the last year. I liked to think of it as the culmination of a journey. Come on you Spurs.
Wednesday
Budget day comes with its own set of rituals. First the photos of the chancellor holding up the red box outside No 11. In the Commons, the budget speech is always preceded by prime minister’s questions. Normally, PMQs are the high spot of the Commons week, but on budget day both the prime minister and the leader of the opposition know that no one is really listening and so they rather just go through the motions. No point in wasting your best lines if no one is going to write them up.
If the budget statement is a tough gig for reporters trying to make an instant assessment of its economic impact, it’s a nightmare for the leader of the opposition. She has to make an instant reply with only what’s already been leaked to back it up. So what you normally get is 20 minutes of “it’s all terrible” and “we wouldn’t have done any of it”. It’s only a day later, when economists and politicians have had a chance to go through the numbers line by line, that a proper assessment can be made.
John Healey isn’t everyone’s go-to guy as the standard bearer for Andy Burnham’s new brand of optimism. His is the voice of despair, a harbinger of the apocalypse. So it was hard going listening to him rattle off 98 not very big measures designed to help with the cost of living through what is forecast to be the toughest decade for the country on record. Healey said he was trying to give everyone some “breathing space”. Very Gen Z. Everyone wants some breathing space these days. But it sounded most that it was the government that needed the breathing space, with the tricky decisions on defence and the welfare bill parked until the next budget. Or the election. Whichever comes sooner.
One person who wasn’t in the Commons to hear the budget was Nigel Farage. He claimed someone had moved his prayer card. This sounded about as plausible as Burnham claiming he couldn’t make it to PMQs because Lucy Powell had taken his seat. If a party leader needs a seat, one can always be found. At the very least, a junior MP is told to make way. If Nige wasn’t in the Commons, it was because he couldn’t be bothered to turn up.
Thursday
It’s amazing how quickly the unbearable becomes bearable. When we first started to go to the Marsden in Sutton for Jill’s chemo, it all seemed overwhelming and terrifying. Today, as we went back for the latest round, it feels if not comfortable then reassuringly familiar. Jill sometimes sleeps, sometimes reads a book on her Kindle, during the infusions. I sit beside her and watch the proceedings in parliament and write the sketch and diary. Like now. The wifi is better than at home. The Oak Centre, where the treatment takes place, is modern and state-of-the-art. More like what I imagine the BA business class lounge at Heathrow to be. A friend whose husband has Alzheimer’s couldn’t believe just how welcoming the centre was. There’s so much more money being invested in cancer than there is in dementia. The best time for a chemo slot is first thing in the morning. That way you can be sure to get a parking slot – free if you are having treatment – and you can also get a window bay in the centre.
For the staff, nothing is ever too much trouble: you never feel as if you are being rushed and they are happy to talk through your fears. Every patient facing their worst nightmare and being held and understood. Made safe. You can always tell where the other patients are in their cycle. There was the Indian woman with the most beautiful hair, hoping the cold cap would do its job. It probably wouldn’t. Then there was the middle-aged bloke who arrived, said hello to the nurses and was asleep in minutes. You could hear the snores from the other end of the room. Best of all is the trolley offering free drinks and sandwiches. It’s staffed by volunteers. My favourite is Sandra who joined the team having been a patient first. Another friend, whose wife died of cancer a few years ago, still volunteers at the hospice where she had palliative care. He makes cocktails for everyone once a week. I call that style.
Friday
My bad. Having previously raved about Celebrity Traitors, I feel somewhat embarrassed to say I have changed my mind. Halfway through last Friday’s episode, I realised not just that I was no longer enjoying myself but also that the celebs were actively irritating me. The whole format suddenly felt tired. As if the show had come to the end of its shelf life mid-run. I no longer cared what happened during the missions, murders and banishments. I just wanted someone – anyone – to go as soon as possible. I didn’t want to hear one more celeb saying “I really love you. We’re going to be best friends for life” when the only time they are likely to meet in the future is on a panel show.
James Acaster’s round table admission of guilt was an epic failure of self-awareness. The claim that he had been playing the game as “faithful” traitor was comically absurd. He had lasted that long precisely because he had played a traitor’s game so well. Mind you, I am planning to watch to the end, out of sheer “I’ve started so I will finish” bloody-mindedness. But the producers do need to think of ways of refreshing the look for next year’s version or it won’t be just me who is bored. I still think there is potential for a politicians version. If you’re near Worcester on 26 November, come to my show at Huntingdon Hall. We can try to make it happen.
-

title: US midterms: Pope Leo XIV casts vote by mail
content_c:
US midterms: Pope Leo XIV casts vote by mail
October 30, 2026
Pope Leo XIV has become the first ever pontiff to vote in a United States general election after submitting a mail-in ballot ahead of November's midterms, the Vatican confirmed on Friday.
The 71-year-old US citizen, who was born in Chicago, Illinois, as Robert Francis Prevost, applied for a postal vote on October 3, according to US media.
The Holy See's press office said in a statement that the pope "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen" and has done so "whenever he was eligible to do so."
Indeed, records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections show that Robert Prevost has voted in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022, including five primary elections.
Through his time as a bishop in Peru, Pope Leo also holds Peruvian citizenship and the Vatican said he had also voted whenever eligible while living in the South American country.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," said a spokesperson in Vatican City, which itself is an absolute monarchy and does not hold political elections.
Pope Leo XIV: Do we know who the pontiff voted for?
In Tuesday's US midterm elections, all seats in the House of Representatives and about one third of the Senate are set to be contested.
US President Donald Trump's Republicans are seeking to defend narrow majorities in both chambers against a strong challenge from the Democrats.
In Illinois, voters are deciding whether to elect Governor JB Pritzker for a third term, and are also filling an open US Senate seat after the retirement of longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin.
It remains unclear who Pope Leo has voted for but the pontiff has repeatedly clashed with President Trump and his administration since the start of his pontificate a year and a half ago.
Leo has criticized Trump on issues such as the Iran war, migration and press freedom and declined an invitation to the United States' 250th anniversary celebrations earlier this year.
The two are yet to meet personally but Trump has often attacked the pontiff personally, calling him "weak" and captive to the "radical left."
"I'm not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for," Leo responded while on a trip to Algeria in April.
"I will continue to speak out strongly against war, seeking to promote peace, promoting dialogue and multilateralism among states to find solutions to problems."
description: As a US citizen, Pope Leo XIV is eligible to vote in US elections and has made use of that right with a postal ballot ahead of Tuesday's midterms. The pontiff, a Chicago native, did not reveal who he voted for.

title: Ebola: Mehr als 5000 Tote in Demokratischer Republik Kongo
content_c:
Opferzahlen steigen weiter Mehr als 5000 Ebola-Tote in Demokratischer Republik Kongo
Die Zahl der Todesopfer des Ebolaausbruchs in der Demokratischen Republik Kongo hat laut Regierungsangaben die Marke von 5000 überschritten. Den Behörden gelingt es weiterhin nicht, die tödlichste Ebolaepidemie in der Geschichte des Landes einzudämmen.
Seit dem Bekanntwerden des Ausbruchs im Mai haben sich mehr als 10.000 Menschen infiziert. Bis heute gibt es keine zugelassenen Behandlungsmethoden oder Impfstoffe gegen den seltenen Virustyp Bundibugyo, der für den Ausbruch in dem zentralafrikanischen Land verantwortlich ist.
Die diesjährige Epidemie wird nur von dem Ausbruch von 2014 bis 2016 übertroffen, bei dem sich über 28.600 Menschen infizierten und mehr als 11.000 Menschen in Guinea, Liberia und Sierra Leone starben.
Bisher sind acht der 26 Provinzen des Kongo betroffen, wobei viele Todesfälle außerhalb von Behandlungszentren zu verzeichnen sind. Vergangene Woche hatte Nigeria als viertes afrikanisches Land im aktuellen Ausbruch einen Ebolafall gemeldet. Auch in den ostafrikanischen Ländern Kenia und Uganda wurden Erkrankte registriert.
description: Bei einem der schwersten Ebolaausbrüche bisher sind in der Demokratischen Republik Kongo inzwischen mehr als 5000 Menschen gestorben. Auch Nigeria, Kenia und Uganda sind betroffen.
